questions.q: In Year 1, Gale Co. sold 1,000 units at $500 each, each with a one-year assurance-type warranty. Warranty costs are estimated at 3% of sales. Gale spent $6,000 on warranty claims in Year 1. What warranty expense and year-end warranty liability should Gale report for Year 1?
choices: Expense $15,000; liability $15,000
Expense $6,000; liability $0
Expense $15,000; liability $9,000
Expense $9,000; liability $9,000
questions.exp: Assurance-type warranty costs are accrued when the sale is made: $500,000 x 3% = $15,000 expense; the liability is reduced by the $6,000 spent, leaving $9,000. Expensing only claims paid is the cash basis, which is not acceptable when costs are probable and estimable.

questions.q: Hazel Co. learned of a product defect that has injured customers, but no claims have yet been filed. Under ASC 450, when is disclosure of this unasserted claim required?
choices: When it is probable that a claim will be asserted and an unfavorable outcome is at least reasonably possible
Always, because any unasserted claim must be disclosed
Only when a claim is formally asserted
Never, because unasserted claims are by definition remote
questions.exp: Disclosure of an unasserted claim is not required unless it is probable that it will be asserted and an unfavorable outcome is reasonably possible (ASC 450-20-50-6). Waiting for formal assertion ignores this probable-assertion test.

questions.q: Ivy Co. guaranteed the bank debt of an unrelated supplier for a fee. At inception, the likelihood that Ivy will have to pay under the guarantee is remote. How should Ivy account for the guarantee at inception?
choices: Accrue the maximum potential payment
No recognition or disclosure, because payment is remote
Recognize a liability for the fair value of its stand-ready obligation and disclose the guarantee
Disclose the guarantee only
questions.exp: Under ASC 460-10, a guarantor recognizes a liability at inception for the fair value of the obligation it undertakes, even if payment is remote, and guarantees are disclosed despite remote likelihood. Omitting disclosure applies the general remote rule, which has an exception for guarantees.

questions.q: Juno Co. faces an environmental claim. Counsel believes a loss is probable but cannot estimate the amount, even as a range, at this time. How should Juno report the claim?
choices: Accrue a nominal amount
Disclose the contingency and state that an estimate cannot be made
Accrue a loss equal to the amount claimed
Make no accrual or disclosure until an estimate can be made
questions.exp: Accrual requires both that a loss be probable and that it be reasonably estimable. When it cannot be estimated, the contingency is disclosed with a statement that an estimate cannot be made (ASC 450-20-50-4). Omitting disclosure would hide a probable loss.

questions.q: During Year 1, Kale Co. issued 100,000 coupons redeemable for a premium that costs Kale $2 net per redemption. Kale expects 30% of the coupons to be redeemed. During Year 1, 12,000 coupons were redeemed. What liability for unredeemed coupons should Kale report at year-end?
questions.exp: Expected redemptions = 30,000; remaining = 30,000 - 12,000 = 18,000 coupons x $2 = $36,000. $60,000 is total expected cost before redemptions, and $18,000 counts coupons, not dollars.

questions.q: Lind Co. chose not to buy property insurance and is exposed to the risk of future fire damage to its buildings. No fire has occurred. How should Lind account for this exposure?
choices: Do not accrue a loss, because no asset has been impaired and no liability incurred at the balance sheet date
Appropriate retained earnings through a charge to income
Accrue a liability equal to the premium that would have been paid
Accrue an estimated annual loss based on industry fire statistics
questions.exp: ASC 450-20-25 does not permit accruals for future losses from uninsured risks because no asset has been impaired or liability incurred as of the balance sheet date. Disclosure of the exposure may be appropriate, but an accrual based on averages is not.

questions.q: Mesa Co. accrued a probable and reasonably estimable $500,000 environmental remediation liability. It also has an insurance claim, which is probable of recovery, for $200,000 of those costs. How should Mesa report these amounts?
choices: Liability of $300,000 with a $200,000 gain contingency disclosed
Liability of $500,000 with the recovery disclosed but not recognized
Liability of $500,000 and a separate receivable of $200,000
Net liability of $300,000
questions.exp: Probable recoveries are recognized as a separate asset; offsetting the liability is generally not appropriate because the right of setoff criteria are not met (ASC 410-30-45). Netting to $300,000 understates both the obligation and the asset.

questions.q: On February 5, Year 2, before its Year 1 statements were issued, Nyx Co. issued $5,000,000 of 10-year bonds. How should Nyx report the bond issuance in its Year 1 financial statements?
choices: Record a receivable for the bond proceeds
No disclosure is required
Disclose the issuance as a nonrecognized subsequent event
Record the bonds as a Year 1 liability
questions.exp: The issuance of debt after the balance sheet date did not exist at year-end, so it is a nonrecognized subsequent event, disclosed if material to keep the statements from being misleading (ASC 855-10-55-2). Recording it in Year 1 treats it as a recognized event.

questions.q: In November, Year 1, a customer was injured on Opal Co.'s premises. The customer sued on January 20, Year 2, before Opal's Year 1 statements were issued, and counsel concludes that a $150,000 loss is probable. How should Opal report the claim in its Year 1 statements?
choices: Accrue the $150,000 loss at December 31, Year 1
Recognize the loss in Year 2 when the suit is settled
Disclose only, because the suit was filed after year-end
Make no disclosure, because no suit existed at year-end
questions.exp: The injury, the underlying cause, occurred before the balance sheet date, so the condition existed at year-end. The suit filed later is a recognized subsequent event, and the probable, estimable loss is accrued (ASC 855-10-55-1). The filing date does not control.

questions.q: Pine Co. reissues its previously issued financial statements in a revised form. Regarding events that occurred after the original issuance date, what should Pine do?
choices: Disclose none of the events, because the original statements control
Recognize all events through the reissuance date
Not recognize events after the original issuance unless required by GAAP or regulatory requirements, and disclose the date through which subsequent events were evaluated in the revised statements
Recognize only events that are favorable
questions.exp: Under ASC 855-10-25-4, an entity does not recognize events occurring between the original issuance and reissuance unless GAAP or regulatory requirements call for it, and revised statements disclose the date through which subsequent events were evaluated. Recognizing everything through the reissuance date ignores this rule.

questions.q: At year-end, Quill Co. faces three lawsuits. Suit 1: loss probable, best estimate $100,000. Suit 2: loss reasonably possible, estimated at $250,000. Suit 3: loss probable, range $50,000 to $150,000 with no best estimate. What total loss should Quill accrue?
questions.exp: Accrue the $100,000 best estimate for Suit 1 and the $50,000 minimum of the range for Suit 3; Suit 2 is only disclosed. Total = $150,000. $400,000 also accrues the reasonably possible suit, which only requires disclosure.

questions.q: At year-end, a foreign government has formally announced that it will expropriate Rook Co.'s facilities in its country, and Rook can reasonably estimate the uncompensated loss at $2,000,000. How should Rook report the expropriation?
choices: Accrue the $2,000,000 loss
Recognize the loss when the assets are seized
Recognize the loss in other comprehensive income
Disclose only, because expropriation is a political event
questions.exp: Threat of expropriation is a loss contingency under ASC 450-20; when expropriation is imminent (probable) and the loss is reasonably estimable, it is accrued. Waiting until the seizure ignores the accrual criteria.

questions.q: Sand Co. holds equity securities measured at fair value. Shortly after year-end, before its statements were issued, a broad market decline reduced their fair value by 30%. How should Sand report the decline?
choices: Recognize the decline in other comprehensive income at year-end
Ignore the decline completely
Disclose the decline as a nonrecognized subsequent event, if material
Adjust the year-end fair value to reflect the decline
questions.exp: Changes in fair value after the balance sheet date reflect conditions arising after that date, so they are nonrecognized subsequent events disclosed if material (ASC 855-10-55-2). Adjusting year-end values would record conditions that did not exist then.

questions.q: On February 1, Year 2, before its Year 1 statements were issued, Tern Co.'s board approved and signed an agreement to sell one of its business segments. How should Tern report the agreement in its Year 1 statements?
choices: Report the segment as a discontinued operation in Year 1
No disclosure is required until the sale closes
Disclose it as a nonrecognized subsequent event
Classify the segment as held for sale at December 31, Year 1
questions.exp: The held-for-sale criteria were not met at year-end, so the decision is a nonrecognized subsequent event, disclosed if material. Classifying the segment as held for sale or discontinued in Year 1 would apply criteria that were met only after the balance sheet date.

questions.q: Una Co. sold 100 machines for $1,200 each. Each sale includes a separately priced 2-year extended warranty (a service-type warranty). The standalone selling prices are $1,000 for the machine and $200 for the extended warranty. How should Una account for the extended warranties at the time of sale?
choices: Recognize all $120,000 as revenue with no warranty accounting
Recognize a $20,000 contract liability, recognized as revenue over the warranty period
Recognize revenue of $120,000 and a warranty liability of $20,000
Accrue warranty expense and a warranty liability of $20,000
questions.exp: A service-type warranty is a separate performance obligation under ASC 606; the $20,000 allocated to it (100 x $200) is deferred and recognized over the coverage period. Accruing an expense is the treatment for an assurance-type warranty.

questions.q: Vega Co. has a noncancelable, unhedged commitment to buy raw materials for $500,000 next year. At year-end, the market price of the materials has fallen to $420,000, and the loss is expected to be realized. What should Vega report at year-end?
choices: Disclosure of the commitment only
A loss of $80,000 and a liability of $80,000
No loss until the materials are purchased
A loss of $80,000 in other comprehensive income
questions.exp: Net losses on firm, noncancelable purchase commitments are recognized when they are expected to be realized (ASC 330-10-35-17), with a liability for the commitment. Disclosure alone is appropriate only if no loss is expected.

questions.q: Wake Co.'s December 31, Year 1 inventory included products that, on February 10, Year 2, it learned were obsolete because a competitor's superior product had been launched in November, Year 1. The Year 1 statements had not yet been issued. How should Wake report the obsolescence?
choices: Write down the inventory at December 31, Year 1
Recognize the write-down in Year 2
Disclose it only, because Wake learned of it in Year 2
Report it as a prior-period adjustment in Year 2
questions.exp: The obsolescence resulted from a condition (the competitor's launch) that existed at the balance sheet date, so it is a recognized subsequent event and the inventory is written down at year-end. The date Wake learned of it does not determine the period.

questions.q: Xeno Co. had a $200,000 receivable from a financially healthy customer at December 31, Year 1. On January 25, Year 2, before Xeno's statements were issued, a fire destroyed the customer's uninsured plant, and Xeno now expects to collect nothing. How should Xeno report this in its Year 1 statements?
choices: Write off the receivable at December 31, Year 1
Disclose the event as a nonrecognized subsequent event, if material
Increase the Year 1 allowance by $200,000
Make no disclosure, because the loss occurred in Year 2
questions.exp: The customer was solvent at year-end; the fire created a new condition after the balance sheet date, so the loss is a nonrecognized subsequent event that is disclosed (ASC 855-10-55-2). Compare this with a bankruptcy caused by deterioration before year-end, which is recognized.

questions.q: Yale Co.'s counsel concludes that an unfavorable judgment is probable and estimates the loss at between $300,000 and $700,000, with $450,000 being the best estimate. What amount should Yale accrue?
questions.exp: When an amount within the range is a better estimate than any other, that amount is accrued (ASC 450-20-30-1), here $450,000. The minimum ($300,000) is used only when no amount in the range is a better estimate.

questions.q: For a loss contingency that is reasonably possible, what must the financial statement disclosure include?
choices: Management's probability percentage for the outcome
Only the nature of the contingency
The nature of the contingency and an estimate of the possible loss or range of loss, or a statement that such an estimate cannot be made
The journal entry that would be recorded if the loss occurred
questions.exp: ASC 450-20-50-4 requires disclosure of the nature of the contingency and an estimate of the possible loss or range, or a statement that an estimate cannot be made. Disclosing only the nature is incomplete.

questions.q: How are accrued loss contingencies, such as litigation liabilities, generally measured with respect to the time value of money under U.S. GAAP?
choices: Generally not discounted unless the amount and timing of the cash payments are fixed or reliably determinable
Always discounted at the entity's incremental borrowing rate
Always discounted at the risk-free rate
Discounted only if the payment is due more than 12 months after year-end
questions.exp: In practice under ASC 450, loss contingencies are recorded at undiscounted amounts unless the aggregate amount and timing of payments are fixed or reliably determinable (as with certain environmental obligations under ASC 410-30). Discounting is not required merely because payment is beyond one year.

questions.q: At year-end, no claim has been asserted against Zeta Co., but a regulatory investigation makes it probable that a claim will be asserted, an unfavorable outcome is probable, and the loss can be reasonably estimated at $600,000. How should Zeta report the matter?
choices: Make no accrual or disclosure
Accrue the loss only after the claim is asserted
Accrue a $600,000 loss
Disclose only, because no claim has been asserted
questions.exp: An unasserted claim is accrued when assertion is probable, an unfavorable outcome is probable, and the loss is reasonably estimable; the lack of a formal claim does not prevent accrual (ASC 450-20-25-2). Disclosure only would apply if the outcome were merely reasonably possible.

questions.q: A company has current assets of $200,000 and current liabilities of $100,000. It pays $20,000 of accounts payable in cash. What is the effect on its current ratio and working capital?
choices: Current ratio decreases; working capital is unchanged
Current ratio increases; working capital is unchanged
Current ratio is unchanged; working capital decreases
Both the current ratio and working capital increase
questions.exp: Both current assets and current liabilities fall by $20,000, so working capital stays at $100,000, while the current ratio rises from 2.0 to $180,000 / $80,000 = 2.25. When the ratio exceeds 1, an equal decrease in both numerator and denominator increases it, so assuming it stays unchanged is the common error.

questions.q: A company has current assets of $80,000 and current liabilities of $100,000. It purchases $20,000 of inventory on account. What is the effect on its current ratio?
choices: No effect
Decreases to zero working capital
Decreases
Increases
questions.exp: The ratio moves from $80,000 / $100,000 = 0.80 to $100,000 / $120,000 = 0.83, an increase, because an equal addition to both terms moves a ratio below 1 toward 1. Candidates who assume the ratio is above 1 conclude it decreases, which would be true only in that case.

questions.q: A company had total sales of $1,080,000, of which $900,000 were on credit. Accounts receivable were $140,000 at the beginning of the year and $160,000 at year-end. Using a 360-day year, what is the average collection period (days sales outstanding)?
choices: 60 days
56 days
50 days
64 days
questions.exp: Receivables turnover = credit sales / average receivables = $900,000 / $150,000 = 6.0, so the collection period is 360 / 6 = 60 days. The 50-day figure uses total sales, including cash sales that never create receivables; 64 days uses ending rather than average receivables.

questions.q: A company reports sales of $900,000 and cost of goods sold of $600,000. Inventory was $110,000 at the beginning of the year and $130,000 at year-end. What is the inventory turnover?
choices: 5.0 times
4.6 times
7.5 times
5.45 times
questions.exp: Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory = $600,000 / [($110,000 + $130,000) / 2] = $600,000 / $120,000 = 5.0 times. Using sales gives 7.5 times, which mixes a selling-price numerator with a cost-based denominator.

questions.q: A company's days inventory outstanding is 73 days, days sales outstanding is 40 days, and days payables outstanding is 30 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
choices: 143 days
113 days
63 days
83 days
questions.exp: Cash conversion cycle = days inventory + days receivables - days payables = 73 + 40 - 30 = 83 days. The 113-day figure is the operating cycle, which ignores that supplier credit delays the company's own cash outflow.

questions.q: A company's cost of goods sold was $500,000. Inventory increased from $80,000 to $100,000 during the year, and accounts payable (all for inventory purchases) increased from $60,000 to $70,000. What is the accounts payable turnover based on purchases and average payables?
choices: 8.7 times
8.0 times
7.4 times
7.7 times
questions.exp: Purchases = COGS + ending inventory - beginning inventory = $500,000 + $100,000 - $80,000 = $520,000; average payables = $65,000; turnover = $520,000 / $65,000 = 8.0 times. The 7.7 figure uses cost of goods sold instead of purchases, ignoring the inventory build-up.

questions.q: A company has total liabilities of $400,000 and total stockholders' equity of $600,000. What is its debt-to-equity ratio?
questions.exp: Debt-to-equity = total liabilities / total equity = $400,000 / $600,000 = 0.67. The 0.40 figure is the debt ratio (liabilities / total assets of $1,000,000), a related but different solvency measure.

questions.q: A company reports net income of $120,000, income tax expense of $40,000, and interest expense of $20,000. What is its times-interest-earned ratio?
choices: 6.0 times
8.0 times
9.0 times
7.0 times
questions.exp: Times interest earned = EBIT / interest = ($120,000 + $40,000 + $20,000) / $20,000 = 9.0 times. The 8.0 figure uses pretax income of $160,000 without adding back the interest itself, understating the earnings available to cover interest.

questions.q: A company reports net income of $150,000 and total assets of $2,000,000. Stockholders' equity was $900,000 at the beginning of the year and $1,100,000 at year-end. What is the return on average stockholders' equity?
questions.exp: Return on equity = net income / average equity = $150,000 / [($900,000 + $1,100,000) / 2] = $150,000 / $1,000,000 = 15.0%. The 13.6% figure uses ending equity, and 7.5% is return on total assets.

questions.q: A company has a net profit margin of 8%, total asset turnover of 1.5, and an equity multiplier (average assets / average equity) of 2.0. Using the DuPont model, what is its return on equity?
questions.exp: DuPont ROE = profit margin x asset turnover x equity multiplier = 8% x 1.5 x 2.0 = 24%. The 12% figure is return on assets (8% x 1.5), which omits the effect of financial leverage.

questions.q: A company reports net income of $540,000. It has cumulative preferred stock with annual dividends of $45,000, which were not declared this year. Weighted-average common shares outstanding were 90,000, and 110,000 common shares were outstanding at year-end. What is basic earnings per share?
questions.exp: Basic EPS = (net income - current-year cumulative preferred dividends, whether or not declared) / weighted-average shares = ($540,000 - $45,000) / 90,000 = $5.50. The $6.00 figure fails to subtract the cumulative preferred dividends, and $4.50 divides by year-end shares instead of the weighted average.

questions.q: A company's earnings per share is $5.50, its market price per share is $66, and it paid common dividends of $2.20 per share. What is its dividend payout ratio?
questions.exp: Dividend payout = dividends per share / EPS = $2.20 / $5.50 = 40%. The 3.3% figure is the dividend yield ($2.20 / $66), which uses market price rather than earnings as the denominator.

questions.q: A company has preferred stock with a liquidation value of $500,000 (par $400,000) and $30,000 of dividends in arrears. Total stockholders' equity is $2,500,000, and 100,000 common shares are outstanding. What is book value per common share?
questions.exp: Equity allocated to common = $2,500,000 - $500,000 liquidation value - $30,000 arrearage = $1,970,000, or $19.70 per share. The $20.00 figure omits the dividends in arrears, which preferred holders must receive before common holders.

questions.q: A company reports net sales of $800,000, cost of goods sold of $520,000, and operating expenses of $160,000. What is its gross profit margin?
questions.exp: Gross profit margin = (sales - COGS) / sales = ($800,000 - $520,000) / $800,000 = 35%. The 15% figure is the operating margin after operating expenses, and 53.8% divides gross profit by COGS rather than sales.

questions.q: A company reports net sales of $3,000,000. Total assets were $1,800,000 at the beginning of the year and $2,200,000 at year-end. What is its total asset turnover?
choices: 0.67 times
1.67 times
1.36 times
1.50 times
questions.exp: Asset turnover = net sales / average total assets = $3,000,000 / $2,000,000 = 1.50 times. Using ending assets gives 1.36 times, and 0.67 inverts the ratio.

questions.q: A company's current liabilities are $200,000, its current ratio is 2.5, and its quick ratio is 1.5. Its current assets consist only of cash, accounts receivable and inventory. What is its inventory?
questions.exp: Current assets = 2.5 x $200,000 = $500,000 and quick assets = 1.5 x $200,000 = $300,000, so inventory, the only nonquick current asset, is $500,000 - $300,000 = $200,000. The $300,000 figure is the quick assets, not the inventory.

questions.q: A company with a current ratio greater than 1.0 declares a cash dividend payable next month. What is the effect of the declaration on its current ratio and working capital?
choices: Neither is affected until the dividend is paid
Current ratio increases; working capital decreases
Current ratio decreases; working capital is unchanged
Both the current ratio and working capital decrease
questions.exp: Declaration debits retained earnings and credits dividends payable, a current liability, so working capital decreases and the current ratio falls because only the denominator rises. Waiting for payment is wrong because the liability arises on the declaration date.

questions.q: A company collects $50,000 of accounts receivable. What is the effect on its current ratio and quick ratio?
choices: Neither ratio changes
Both ratios decrease
The current ratio is unchanged and the quick ratio increases
Both ratios increase
questions.exp: Collection exchanges one quick, current asset (receivables) for another (cash), so total current assets, quick assets and current liabilities are all unchanged. Thinking that more cash improves the quick ratio ignores that receivables were already in the quick numerator.

questions.q: Under the allowance method, a company writes off a $10,000 uncollectible account receivable. What is the effect on its current ratio and working capital?
choices: Both increase because the allowance is reduced
Current ratio decreases; working capital is unchanged
Both decrease by the amount of the write-off
Neither is affected
questions.exp: The write-off debits the allowance and credits accounts receivable, so net receivables and total current assets are unchanged. The decrease in current assets happened earlier, when bad debt expense was recorded and the allowance was established.

questions.q: A company with a current ratio greater than 1.0 issues ten-year bonds at par for cash. What is the effect on its current ratio and debt-to-equity ratio?
choices: Current ratio decreases; debt-to-equity increases
Current ratio is unchanged; debt-to-equity increases
Both ratios increase
Current ratio increases; debt-to-equity is unchanged
questions.exp: Cash, a current asset, increases while the bonds are a noncurrent liability, so the current ratio rises; total liabilities increase with no change in equity, so debt-to-equity rises. Treating the bond as having no liquidity effect overlooks the cash received.

questions.q: Holders of a company's convertible bonds convert them into common stock, and no gain or loss is recognized. What is the effect on the company's debt-to-equity ratio and its times-interest-earned ratio for future periods?
choices: Debt-to-equity decreases; times interest earned decreases
Debt-to-equity increases; times interest earned decreases
Debt-to-equity decreases; times interest earned increases
Neither ratio is affected because total capital is unchanged
questions.exp: Conversion moves the bonds' carrying amount from liabilities to equity, lowering debt-to-equity, and eliminates future interest expense, so EBIT covers the remaining interest more times. Total capital is unchanged, but its mix between debt and equity, which these ratios measure, has shifted.

questions.q: A company purchases its own common stock for cash to hold as treasury stock. Assuming net income is unchanged and the current ratio exceeds 1.0, what is the effect on its debt-to-equity ratio and earnings per share?
choices: Debt-to-equity is unchanged; EPS is unchanged
Debt-to-equity increases; EPS increases
Debt-to-equity decreases; EPS increases
Debt-to-equity increases; EPS decreases
questions.exp: Treasury stock reduces total equity with no change in liabilities, raising debt-to-equity, and fewer shares outstanding raises EPS. Candidates sometimes treat treasury stock as an asset, which would leave equity and debt-to-equity unchanged.

questions.q: A company declares and issues a 2-for-1 stock split. What is the effect on its debt-to-equity ratio and its earnings per share?
choices: Debt-to-equity is unchanged; EPS is halved
Both ratios are unchanged
Debt-to-equity decreases; EPS is unchanged
Debt-to-equity increases; EPS is halved
questions.exp: A stock split changes only the number of shares and the par value per share, so total equity and debt-to-equity are unchanged, while doubling the shares halves EPS (prior periods are restated). Thinking equity changes confuses a split with a dividend or a share repurchase.

questions.q: During a period of rising prices, how does a company using LIFO compare with an otherwise identical company using FIFO?
choices: LIFO produces a higher inventory turnover and a lower current ratio
LIFO produces a lower inventory turnover and a higher current ratio
LIFO produces a higher inventory turnover and a higher current ratio
LIFO produces a higher gross margin and a lower inventory turnover
questions.exp: In rising prices LIFO charges newer, higher costs to COGS and leaves older, lower costs in inventory, so the turnover numerator rises and the denominator falls, while lower inventory reduces the current ratio. LIFO lowers rather than raises gross margin when prices rise.

questions.q: A company writes down inventory to net realizable value, charging the loss to cost of goods sold. Assuming the current ratio exceeds 1.0, what is the effect on its current ratio and inventory turnover?
choices: Neither ratio is affected because the write-down is a noncash charge
Current ratio increases; inventory turnover decreases
Current ratio decreases; inventory turnover decreases
Current ratio decreases; inventory turnover increases
questions.exp: The write-down reduces inventory, a current asset, which lowers the current ratio, and it both reduces average inventory and increases COGS, which raises inventory turnover. Being noncash does not prevent a write-down from reducing a balance sheet asset.

questions.q: A company has a current ratio of 3.0 but a quick ratio of only 0.6, while its industry averages are 2.0 and 1.0, respectively. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: A large portion of its current assets is tied up in inventory and other nonquick assets
The company is highly leveraged relative to its industry
The company has more cash than it needs to meet current obligations
The company has excessive accounts receivable relative to sales
questions.exp: The gap between the current and quick ratios is caused by current assets excluded from the quick ratio, chiefly inventory and prepaid items, so the company's liquidity depends on selling its inventory. Excess cash or receivables would raise the quick ratio, not depress it.

questions.q: Which of the following ratios is primarily a measure of long-term solvency rather than short-term liquidity or operating efficiency?
choices: Current ratio
Acid-test ratio
Days sales in accounts receivable
Debt-to-total-assets ratio
questions.exp: Solvency ratios, such as debt-to-total-assets, debt-to-equity and times interest earned, assess the ability to meet long-term obligations and the extent of financial leverage. The acid-test and current ratios measure short-term liquidity, and days sales in receivables is an activity ratio.

questions.q: An analyst wants to compare the cost structures of two companies of very different sizes by expressing each income statement line item as a percentage of net sales. What type of analysis is this?
choices: DuPont analysis
Horizontal (trend) analysis
Ratio analysis of solvency
Vertical (common-size) analysis
questions.exp: Vertical analysis restates each line as a percentage of a base within the same statement, net sales for the income statement or total assets for the balance sheet, which neutralizes size differences. Horizontal analysis instead compares the same line item across periods, often as a percentage change from a base year.

questions.q: Why is the acid-test ratio considered a more stringent test of liquidity than the current ratio?
choices: It includes long-term investments that can be sold if needed
It excludes inventory and prepaid expenses, which are less readily converted into cash
It uses only cash and ignores receivables and marketable securities
It subtracts long-term debt from current assets before dividing by current liabilities
questions.exp: The acid-test ratio limits the numerator to cash, marketable securities and net receivables, excluding inventory, which must first be sold and often collected, and prepaid items, which will never produce cash. A ratio of only cash and cash equivalents to current liabilities is the cash ratio, an even stricter measure.

questions.q: On November 20, Year 1, a U.S. company purchased inventory on account from a German supplier for 100,000 euros, payable on January 15, Year 2. The spot rates were $1.10 on November 20, $1.15 on December 31, and $1.12 on January 15. What foreign currency transaction gain or loss should the company report in its Year 1 income statement?
choices: $2,000 loss
$0, because the payable has not yet been settled
$5,000 gain
$5,000 loss
questions.exp: The euro-denominated payable is remeasured at the year-end spot rate: 100,000 x ($1.15 - $1.10) = $5,000 increase in the liability, which is a transaction loss in Year 1 income. Transaction gains and losses are recognized as rates change, not deferred until settlement, and a rising foreign currency hurts a holder of a foreign-currency payable.

questions.q: On November 15, Year 1, a U.S. company sold goods to a Japanese customer for an amount denominated in a foreign currency (FC) of 200,000 FC, collectible on January 20, Year 2. The spot rates were $0.80 on November 15, $0.78 on December 31, and $0.83 on January 20. What transaction gain or loss should the company report in Year 2?
choices: $4,000 loss
$6,000 gain
questions.exp: At December 31 the receivable was remeasured to 200,000 x $0.78 = $156,000; it was collected for 200,000 x $0.83 = $166,000, a Year 2 gain of $10,000. The $6,000 figure is the total gain over both years measured from the original $160,000, which ignores the $4,000 loss already recognized in Year 1.

questions.q: A U.S. company borrowed 1,000,000 foreign currency units (FC) on July 1, Year 1, when the spot rate was $0.60. The loan is repayable in FC in Year 3. At December 31, Year 1, the spot rate was $0.64. Ignoring interest, what amount should be reported for the loan principal in Year 1 income?
choices: $0, because the loan is noncurrent
questions.exp: The FC loan payable is a monetary liability remeasured at the current rate: 1,000,000 x ($0.64 - $0.60) = $40,000 increase in the dollar liability, a transaction loss in net income. A long-term maturity does not defer recognition, and the strengthening FC makes the debt costlier, so it is a loss, not a gain.

questions.q: A U.S. company purchases equipment from a Canadian supplier, and the invoice is denominated in U.S. dollars. The Canadian dollar weakens against the U.S. dollar between the purchase date and the payment date. How should the U.S. company account for the rate change?
choices: The equipment's cost is adjusted for the change in the exchange rate
A transaction gain is recognized because the Canadian dollar weakened
A transaction loss is recognized in other comprehensive income
No transaction gain or loss is recognized because the payable is fixed in U.S. dollars
questions.exp: A foreign currency transaction exists only when the transaction is denominated in a currency other than the entity's functional currency; a dollar-denominated invoice fixes the U.S. company's obligation, so the exchange risk falls on the supplier. Recognizing a gain treats the invoice as if it were denominated in Canadian dollars.

questions.q: Under ASC 830, where are foreign currency transaction gains and losses on a U.S. company's short-term foreign-currency-denominated receivables and payables generally reported?
choices: As an adjustment to the cost of the related inventory or revenue
As a direct adjustment to retained earnings when settled
In other comprehensive income as part of the cumulative translation adjustment
In net income in the period in which the exchange rate changes
questions.exp: Transaction gains and losses are included in determining net income for the period in which rates change, with limited exceptions such as designated hedges of a net investment and intercompany balances of a long-term-investment nature. The cumulative translation adjustment in OCI arises from translating a foreign entity's statements, not from ordinary transactions.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary keeps its books in its local currency, but its functional currency has been determined to be the U.S. dollar. Which process is used to convert its financial statements for consolidation, and where is the resulting gain or loss reported?
choices: Remeasurement using the temporal method, with the gain or loss reported in net income
Remeasurement using the temporal method, with the gain or loss reported in other comprehensive income
Translation using the current rate method, with the adjustment reported in other comprehensive income
Translation using the current rate method, with the adjustment reported in net income
questions.exp: When books are kept in a currency other than the functional currency, the statements are remeasured into the functional currency using historical rates for nonmonetary items and current rates for monetary items, and remeasurement gains and losses go to net income. Translation with OCI treatment applies only when the local currency is the functional currency.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary's functional currency is its local currency, which is also the currency of its books. When its financial statements are translated into U.S. dollars for consolidation, which exchange rate is used for its assets and liabilities?
choices: The historical rate on the date each asset or liability arose
The weighted-average rate for the year
The current exchange rate at the balance sheet date
The current rate for monetary items and historical rates for nonmonetary items
questions.exp: Under the current rate method, all assets and liabilities are translated at the current rate at the balance sheet date, revenues and expenses at the rates on the transaction dates (or a weighted average), and equity at historical rates. Splitting monetary and nonmonetary items is the remeasurement (temporal) approach used when the U.S. dollar is the functional currency.

questions.q: When a foreign subsidiary's financial statements are translated from its functional currency into U.S. dollars, revenues and expenses incurred evenly throughout the year are most appropriately translated at which rate?
choices: The historical rate on the date the subsidiary was acquired
The current rate at the balance sheet date
The weighted-average exchange rate for the period
The rate at the beginning of the year
questions.exp: ASC 830 requires revenues, expenses, gains and losses to be translated at the rates on the dates they are recognized, and a weighted-average rate for the period is an acceptable practical approximation. The current year-end rate applies to assets and liabilities, not income statement items.

questions.q: A U.S. parent's foreign subsidiary purchased equipment for 500,000 foreign currency units (FC) when the exchange rate was $0.50. At the current year-end the rate is $0.40, and the weighted-average rate for the year was $0.45. The subsidiary's functional currency is the U.S. dollar. Ignoring depreciation, at what amount should the equipment be reported in the consolidated balance sheet?
questions.exp: Because the functional currency is the U.S. dollar, the statements are remeasured, and equipment is a nonmonetary item carried at the historical rate: 500,000 x $0.50 = $250,000. The $200,000 figure uses the current rate, which would apply only if the local currency were the functional currency and the statements were translated.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary whose functional currency is its local currency (LC) had net assets of LC 1,000,000 throughout the year, with no income, dividends or capital transactions. The exchange rate was $1.20 at the beginning of the year and $1.25 at year-end. What translation adjustment results for the year, and where is it reported?
choices: $50,000 gain in other comprehensive income
$50,000 gain in net income
$50,000 loss in other comprehensive income
No adjustment because the net assets in LC did not change
questions.exp: Translated net assets rise from LC 1,000,000 x $1.20 = $1,200,000 to LC 1,000,000 x $1.25 = $1,250,000, a positive $50,000 translation adjustment reported in OCI. Reporting it in net income confuses translation adjustments with remeasurement or transaction gains.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary's functional currency is its local currency (LC). Its translated retained earnings at the beginning of the year were $400,000. Net income for the year was LC 200,000, translated at the weighted-average rate of $1.10, and dividends of LC 50,000 were declared when the rate was $1.12. The year-end rate is $1.15. What is the translated ending retained earnings balance?
questions.exp: Retained earnings is rolled forward in dollars: $400,000 + (LC 200,000 x $1.10) - (LC 50,000 x $1.12) = $400,000 + $220,000 - $56,000 = $564,000. The $565,000 figure translates dividends at the average rate instead of the rate on the declaration date.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary operates in a country whose cumulative inflation over the past three years exceeds 100%. How should the subsidiary's financial statements be converted into U.S. dollars for consolidation?
choices: Remeasure as if the U.S. dollar were the functional currency, with gains and losses in net income
Translate all accounts at the historical rate in effect when the subsidiary was acquired
Restate for general price-level changes and then translate at the current rate
Translate using the current rate method, with adjustments in other comprehensive income
questions.exp: ASC 830 treats a highly inflationary economy's currency as unsuitable as a functional currency, so the reporting currency is used as the functional currency and the statements are remeasured with gains and losses in net income. Translating at the current rate would sharply shrink nonmonetary assets as the local currency collapses, which is the distortion the rule avoids.

questions.q: A foreign subsidiary keeps its books in Mexican pesos, its functional currency is the euro, and its U.S. parent reports in U.S. dollars. How are the subsidiary's statements converted for consolidation?
choices: Remeasured from pesos into euros, with gains and losses in net income, then translated into dollars, with adjustments in other comprehensive income
Translated from pesos into euros, then remeasured from euros into dollars
Remeasured directly from pesos into dollars, with the entire adjustment in net income
Translated directly from pesos into dollars, with the entire adjustment in other comprehensive income
questions.exp: Statements are first remeasured from the bookkeeping currency into the functional currency, with remeasurement gains and losses in net income, and then translated from the functional currency into the reporting currency, with the translation adjustment in OCI. Going directly from pesos to dollars skips the functional currency step that ASC 830 requires.

questions.q: A U.S. parent has an intercompany advance to its foreign subsidiary, denominated in the subsidiary's functional currency, for which settlement is not planned or anticipated in the foreseeable future. How are exchange gains and losses on the advance reported in the consolidated statements?
choices: Deferred until the advance is repaid and then reported in net income
Eliminated entirely on consolidation with no effect on any statement
In net income, like any other foreign currency transaction
In other comprehensive income as part of the translation adjustment
questions.exp: Intercompany foreign currency balances of a long-term-investment nature are an exception to the general rule, and their exchange gains and losses are reported in OCI with the translation adjustment. Reporting them in net income applies to ordinary intercompany balances expected to be settled.

questions.q: Under ASC 815, which of the following is one of the characteristics a contract must have to meet the definition of a derivative instrument?
choices: It requires no initial net investment or one smaller than would be needed for similar market exposure
It must be traded on an organized exchange
It must be designated as a hedge of an identified risk
It must mature within one year of inception
questions.exp: A derivative has one or more underlyings and notional amounts or payment provisions, little or no initial net investment, and terms that permit or require net settlement. Many derivatives, such as forwards and swaps, trade over the counter, and hedge designation affects only the accounting for gains and losses, not whether the contract is a derivative.

questions.q: A company enters into an interest rate swap in which it pays a fixed rate and receives a variable rate based on SOFR on $10,000,000. In this contract, the $10,000,000 and SOFR are, respectively, the
choices: notional amount and payment provision
initial net investment and underlying
underlying and notional amount
notional amount and underlying
questions.exp: The notional amount is the number of currency units or other units specified in the contract, and the underlying is the variable, such as an interest rate or price, that is applied to the notional amount to determine settlement. Candidates often reverse the two terms because both are needed to compute the swap payments.

questions.q: How should a company that holds a derivative not designated as a hedging instrument measure and report it?
choices: Off the balance sheet, with disclosure of the notional amount
At cost, with gains and losses recognized only at settlement
At fair value on the balance sheet, with changes in fair value recognized in other comprehensive income
At fair value on the balance sheet, with changes in fair value recognized in net income
questions.exp: ASC 815 requires all derivatives to be recognized as assets or liabilities at fair value, and changes in the fair value of derivatives not designated in a qualifying hedge are recognized currently in earnings. OCI treatment is available only for qualifying cash flow hedges and net investment hedges.

questions.q: On November 1, a company with no hedging objective entered into a 90-day forward contract to buy 100,000 foreign currency units (FC) at a forward rate of $1.50. On December 31, the forward rate for delivery on the contract's settlement date was $1.54. Ignoring discounting, what should the company report at December 31?
choices: No asset and no gain until the contract is settled
A $154,000 asset and a $154,000 liability
A $4,000 asset and a $4,000 gain in other comprehensive income
A $4,000 asset and a $4,000 gain in net income
questions.exp: The right to buy FC at $1.50 when the forward rate is $1.54 is worth 100,000 x ($1.54 - $1.50) = $4,000, reported as an asset with the change recognized in earnings because the contract is speculative. OCI treatment requires a designated, qualifying cash flow hedge.

questions.q: On October 1, a company paid a $3,000 premium for a purchased call option on a stock index; the option is not designated as a hedge. At December 31, the option's fair value is $5,000. What amount should the company recognize in net income for the year related to the option?
choices: $5,000 gain
$3,000 expense
$2,000 gain
$0 until the option is exercised or expires
questions.exp: The premium is recorded as an asset at its $3,000 cost, and the derivative is then adjusted to fair value with changes in earnings: $5,000 - $3,000 = $2,000 gain. Recognizing $5,000 ignores that the company paid $3,000 for the option at inception.

questions.q: A company designates a futures contract as a fair value hedge of commodity inventory it holds. During the year, the fair value of the inventory attributable to the hedged risk decreased by $30,000 and the fair value of the futures contract increased by $28,000. What is the net effect of these changes on the company's earnings for the year?
choices: $30,000 decrease
$2,000 decrease
$28,000 increase
No effect, because the hedge is highly effective
questions.exp: In a fair value hedge, both the change in the derivative's fair value and the change in the hedged item's fair value attributable to the hedged risk are recognized in earnings: $28,000 gain - $30,000 loss = $2,000 net decrease. Being highly effective qualifies the hedge for hedge accounting but does not make any imperfect offset disappear.

questions.q: In a qualifying fair value hedge of fixed-rate debt using an interest rate swap, how is the carrying amount of the hedged debt affected?
choices: It is adjusted to full fair value, with the offset recognized in other comprehensive income
It is reduced by the swap's fair value so that the net liability equals the debt's face amount
It is adjusted for the change in fair value attributable to the hedged risk, with the offset recognized in earnings
It is not changed; only the swap is adjusted to fair value
questions.exp: Fair value hedge accounting adjusts the hedged item's carrying amount for changes in fair value attributable to the hedged risk, with that adjustment recognized in earnings to offset the derivative's gain or loss. Leaving the debt unchanged describes the accounting for a derivative that is not designated in a hedge.

questions.q: A company designates a forward contract as a cash flow hedge of a forecasted inventory purchase. Under current GAAP, how are changes in the fair value of the hedging instrument included in the assessment of hedge effectiveness reported before the forecasted transaction affects earnings?
choices: As an adjustment to the carrying amount of the forecasted inventory
Only in the notes until the purchase occurs
In other comprehensive income, to be reclassified into earnings when the hedged transaction affects earnings
In net income immediately
questions.exp: For a cash flow hedge, the change in fair value of the hedging instrument included in the effectiveness assessment is recorded in OCI and later reclassified to earnings, in the same income statement line as the hedged item, when the hedged transaction affects earnings. Immediate earnings recognition is fair value hedge or non-hedge treatment.

questions.q: On November 1, a company designated a forward contract as a cash flow hedge of a forecasted purchase of inventory in February. At December 31, the forward contract had a fair value of $12,000, all of which is included in the assessment of effectiveness, and the hedge is highly effective. What is the effect on the company's year-end financial statements?
choices: $12,000 asset; $12,000 reduction of inventory cost
$12,000 asset; $12,000 gain in other comprehensive income; no effect on net income
No asset; $12,000 disclosed in the notes
$12,000 asset; $12,000 gain in net income
questions.exp: The forward is recognized at its $12,000 fair value, and because it is an effective cash flow hedge of a transaction that has not yet affected earnings, the gain goes to OCI. Inventory cannot be adjusted at year-end because the purchase has not occurred yet.

questions.q: A company recorded a $12,000 gain in accumulated other comprehensive income on a cash flow hedge of a forecasted inventory purchase. The inventory was purchased in February of Year 2 and sold in August of Year 2. When and where should the $12,000 be reclassified into earnings?
choices: In August, as a reduction of cost of goods sold when the inventory is sold
In February, as other income when the inventory is purchased
It remains in accumulated other comprehensive income permanently
In August, as other income separate from cost of goods sold
questions.exp: Amounts in AOCI from a cash flow hedge are reclassified when the hedged forecasted transaction affects earnings, which for inventory is when it is sold and charged to cost of goods sold, and they are presented in the same line item as the hedged item. Reclassifying at purchase is premature because buying inventory does not affect earnings.

questions.q: A company has a cash flow hedge of a forecasted sale, with a $9,000 loss in accumulated other comprehensive income. Management now concludes that it is probable the forecasted sale will not occur. What should the company do with the $9,000?
choices: Transfer it directly to retained earnings
Leave it in accumulated other comprehensive income until the derivative is settled
Amortize it into earnings over the derivative's remaining term
Reclassify it into earnings immediately
questions.exp: When it becomes probable that a forecasted transaction will not occur, the related gains or losses in AOCI are reclassified into earnings immediately because there will be no future earnings effect to offset. Leaving the amount in AOCI is appropriate only while the transaction remains reasonably possible to occur.

questions.q: A company expects to purchase 50,000 barrels of oil next quarter but has not entered into any purchase contract. It wants to hedge the risk that oil prices will rise before it buys. Which type of hedge can it designate?
choices: Either a fair value hedge or a cash flow hedge, at the company's choice
A hedge of a net investment in a foreign operation
A cash flow hedge, because the exposure is variability in the cash flows of a forecasted transaction
A fair value hedge, because oil has a readily determinable market price
questions.exp: A forecasted transaction is not a recognized asset or liability or a firm commitment, so it has no fair value exposure to hedge; its exposure is variability in future cash flows, which qualifies only for cash flow hedge accounting. The choice between fair value and cash flow hedging arises only for certain foreign currency exposures, such as a firm commitment or a recognized foreign-currency-denominated asset or liability.

questions.q: A company with variable-rate debt enters into a swap in which it receives a variable rate and pays a fixed rate, effectively converting the debt to fixed-rate. How should the swap be designated if hedge accounting is elected?
choices: As a fair value hedge of a firm commitment
As a fair value hedge of the debt
As a cash flow hedge of the variability in interest payments
As a hedge of a net investment in a foreign operation
questions.exp: Variable-rate debt has fixed fair value but variable interest cash flows, so a pay-fixed, receive-variable swap hedges cash flow variability and is a cash flow hedge. A fair value hedge applies to the reverse case, where fixed-rate debt is swapped to variable to hedge changes in the debt's fair value.

questions.q: A U.S. company enters into a firm commitment to purchase machinery from a Swiss supplier for a price fixed in Swiss francs, to be paid in six months. It enters into a forward contract to buy francs to hedge the exchange risk. How may the forward contract be designated?
choices: Only as a cash flow hedge, because the payment will occur in the future
As either a fair value hedge or a cash flow hedge of the foreign currency risk
Only as a fair value hedge, because a firm commitment is involved
It cannot be designated, because unrecognized firm commitments are not eligible hedged items
questions.exp: ASC 815 permits the foreign currency exposure in an unrecognized firm commitment to be designated as either a fair value hedge or a cash flow hedge. Restricting it to a fair value hedge is correct for firm commitments exposed to other risks, such as price risk, but not for foreign currency risk.

questions.q: A U.S. parent borrows in euros and designates the euro-denominated debt as a hedge of its net investment in a German subsidiary whose functional currency is the euro. The hedge is effective. Where are exchange gains and losses on the debt reported?
choices: Deferred on the balance sheet until the debt is repaid
As an adjustment to the carrying amount of the investment in the subsidiary
In other comprehensive income as part of the cumulative translation adjustment
In net income as foreign currency transaction gains and losses
questions.exp: Gains and losses on an effective hedge of a net investment in a foreign operation are reported in OCI with the cumulative translation adjustment, offsetting the translation adjustment on the net investment. Without the net investment hedge designation, gains and losses on the euro debt would be transaction gains and losses in net income.

questions.q: A company's hedging relationship produced a $90,000 gain on the derivative and a $100,000 loss on the hedged item attributable to the hedged risk. Under the commonly applied 80%-125% guideline, how should the hedge's effectiveness be evaluated?
choices: Not highly effective, because the derivative gain was smaller than the hedged item loss
Not highly effective, because the offset is less than 100%
Highly effective only if management documents it after the period ends
Highly effective, because the 90% offset falls within the 80%-125% range
questions.exp: The offset ratio is $90,000 / $100,000 = 90%, inside the 80%-125% range generally used to judge a hedge highly effective, and effectiveness must be documented and assessed from inception rather than after the fact. A perfect 100% offset is not required for hedge accounting.

questions.q: Which measurement focus and basis of accounting are used for a city's governmental fund financial statements?
choices: Current financial resources measurement focus and cash basis
Economic resources measurement focus and accrual basis
Current financial resources measurement focus and modified accrual basis
Economic resources measurement focus and modified accrual basis
questions.exp: Governmental funds (general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service, permanent) use the current financial resources focus and modified accrual basis. The economic resources focus with accrual basis is used for government-wide, proprietary, and fiduciary statements.

questions.q: For the year, Elm City levied property taxes of $1,000,000, of which 2% is estimated to be uncollectible. It collected $900,000 during the year and expects to collect $50,000 within 60 days after year-end and the remaining $30,000 later in the following year. What property tax revenue should the general fund report?
questions.exp: Under modified accrual, property tax revenue is recognized when measurable and available; available means collected within the period or soon enough after (generally 60 days) to pay current liabilities: $900,000 + $50,000 = $950,000. The $30,000 is a deferred inflow; $980,000 is the government-wide amount.

questions.q: Which funds are excluded from a state or local government's government-wide financial statements?
choices: Fiduciary funds
Internal service funds
Permanent funds
Enterprise funds
questions.exp: Government-wide statements report governmental and business-type activities of the primary government and its component units; fiduciary activities are excluded because the resources cannot support the government's own programs (GASB 34). Internal service funds are generally folded into governmental activities rather than excluded.

questions.q: The general fund of Oak County issued a purchase order for supplies estimated at $5,000 and recorded an encumbrance. The supplies arrived with an invoice for $5,100. What entries should be recorded when the supplies are received?
choices: Debit supplies inventory $5,100; credit encumbrances $5,100
Debit expenditures $5,000; credit vouchers payable $5,000
Reverse the $5,000 encumbrance; debit expenditures and credit vouchers payable for $5,100
Reverse the $5,100 encumbrance; debit expenditures $5,000
questions.exp: On receipt, the original encumbrance ($5,000) is reversed and the expenditure is recorded at the actual invoice amount ($5,100). Recording the expenditure at the estimate ignores the actual cost of the goods.

questions.q: At the start of the year, a city's general fund recorded its annual budget with estimated revenues of $5,000,000 and appropriations of $4,800,000. What budgetary entry is made to balance the entry?
choices: Credit unassigned fund balance $200,000
Debit encumbrances $200,000
Debit budgetary fund balance $200,000
Credit budgetary fund balance $200,000
questions.exp: Estimated revenues are debited ($5,000,000) and appropriations credited ($4,800,000); the expected surplus is credited to budgetary fund balance for $200,000. Budgetary entries do not affect the actual unassigned fund balance.

questions.q: A city's general fund paid $60,000 cash for a new police vehicle. How is the purchase reported in the general fund statements and in the government-wide statements?
choices: General fund: $60,000 expenditure; government-wide: $60,000 capital asset, depreciated over its useful life
Both: $60,000 expenditure
Both: $60,000 capital asset
General fund: $60,000 capital asset; government-wide: $60,000 expense
questions.exp: Governmental funds report capital outlays as expenditures because they use current financial resources; the government-wide statements (economic resources focus) capitalize and depreciate the vehicle. Capitalizing it in the general fund mixes the two measurement focuses.

questions.q: The city council passed an ordinance, its highest level of decision-making authority, requiring that $400,000 of general fund resources be used only for park improvements; the ordinance can be changed only by another ordinance. How should the $400,000 be classified in the general fund's fund balance?
choices: Restricted
Committed
Nonspendable
Assigned
questions.exp: Under GASB 54, amounts constrained by formal action of the government's highest decision-making authority are committed. Restricted requires constraints imposed externally (creditors, grantors, laws of other governments) or by enabling legislation, and assigned reflects intent by a lesser authority.

questions.q: A city operates a water utility financed primarily by user charges set to recover costs, including capital costs. In which fund should the utility be reported?
choices: General fund
Enterprise fund
Internal service fund
Special revenue fund
questions.exp: Activities that charge fees to external users for goods or services, especially when costs are recovered through fees, are reported in enterprise funds (GASB 34). Internal service funds serve other departments of the government, not the public.

questions.q: A county's central motor pool provides vehicles to other county departments on a cost-reimbursement basis. How are the motor pool's activities generally reported?
choices: In a custodial fund
In the general fund
In an internal service fund, with its balances generally included in governmental activities in the government-wide statements
In an enterprise fund, and as business-type activities in the government-wide statements
questions.exp: Services provided to other departments on a cost-reimbursement basis are reported in internal service funds; because they mainly serve governmental funds, their assets and liabilities are usually included in governmental activities on the government-wide statements. Enterprise funds serve external customers.

questions.q: A city has $4,000,000 of 5% general obligation bonds, with interest payable semiannually on January 1 and July 1. The city's fiscal year ends December 31, and no resources have been accumulated in the debt service fund for the January 1 payment. How should accrued interest be reported at December 31?
choices: Debt service fund: $100,000 accrued; government-wide: none
Neither reports interest until it is paid on January 1
Debt service fund: no interest accrued; government-wide: $100,000 of interest payable
Both report $100,000 of interest payable
questions.exp: Under modified accrual, interest on general long-term debt is generally recognized as an expenditure when due, so the debt service fund accrues nothing; the government-wide statements accrue six months of interest, $4,000,000 x 5% x 6/12 = $100,000. Accruing it in the fund ignores the when-due exception.

questions.q: A city issued $5,000,000 of general obligation bonds at 102 to finance a new library. The proceeds were recorded in a capital projects fund. How should the issuance be reported in the capital projects fund?
choices: Bonds payable of $5,100,000
Other financing sources totaling $5,100,000 (bond proceeds and premium)
Other financing sources of $5,000,000 and revenue of $100,000
Other financing sources of $5,000,000 and a deferred inflow of $100,000
questions.exp: Governmental funds report bond proceeds, including any premium, as other financing sources, not liabilities: $5,000,000 + $100,000 = $5,100,000. Bonds payable are reported only in the government-wide statements.

questions.q: A donor gave a city $1,000,000, stipulating that the principal be held permanently and the earnings be used to maintain the city's public cemetery. In which fund should the city report the resources?
choices: Special revenue fund
Custodial fund
Private-purpose trust fund
Permanent fund
questions.exp: A permanent fund reports resources legally restricted so that only earnings may be used to support the government's own programs, such as perpetual care of a public cemetery (GASB 54). A private-purpose trust is used when the earnings benefit individuals, private organizations, or other governments.

questions.q: Under GASB 84, a county collects property taxes on behalf of school districts and other governments and remits them. The assets are not held in a trust. In which type of fund should the county report these activities?
choices: Agency fund
Custodial fund
Private-purpose trust fund
General fund
questions.exp: GASB 84 replaced agency funds with custodial funds for fiduciary activities not held in a trust that meets specified criteria. Custodial funds report a statement of fiduciary net position and a statement of changes in fiduciary net position.

questions.q: At year-end, a city's employees had earned $500,000 of vested vacation leave. Of that amount, $20,000 is owed to employees who retired before year-end and will be paid in the next month. What liability for compensated absences should the general fund report?
questions.exp: Governmental funds report compensated absences liabilities only for amounts that have matured (are due and payable), here the $20,000 owed to retired employees. The full $500,000 is reported in the government-wide statements.

questions.q: Under GASB 34, when may a government elect not to depreciate its eligible infrastructure assets (the modified approach)?
choices: Whenever the infrastructure is financed with general obligation bonds
When it uses an asset management system and documents that the assets are preserved at or above an established condition level
Whenever the infrastructure has an indefinite useful life
Only for infrastructure acquired before GASB 34 was adopted
questions.exp: The modified approach is allowed for eligible infrastructure if the government manages the assets using an asset management system and documents that they are maintained at or above the condition level it establishes; preservation costs are then expensed instead of depreciation. Funding source and acquisition date do not qualify an asset.

questions.q: How is management's discussion and analysis (MD&A) classified in a state or local government's financial report under GASB 34?
choices: As part of the statistical section
As part of the basic financial statements
As required supplementary information
As other supplementary information
questions.exp: MD&A is required supplementary information (RSI) that precedes the basic financial statements. RSI is not part of the basic statements, but auditors apply limited procedures to it.

questions.q: A city's general fund transferred $300,000 to its debt service fund to pay principal and interest on general obligation bonds. How should the transaction be reported in the governmental fund statements?
choices: General fund expenditure; debt service fund revenue
General fund interfund receivable; debt service fund interfund payable
General fund other financing use (transfer out); debt service fund other financing source (transfer in)
No entry until the bonds are paid
questions.exp: A nonreciprocal flow of resources between funds with no expectation of repayment is an interfund transfer, reported as other financing uses and sources (GASB 34). Treating it as expenditure and revenue would double count.

questions.q: A city's general fund paid the city's water enterprise fund $30,000 for water used by city offices, at the same rates charged to other customers. How should the transaction be reported in the fund statements?
choices: No entry, because it is within the same government
General fund expenditure of $30,000; enterprise fund operating revenue of $30,000
General fund transfer out; enterprise fund transfer in
General fund reduction of an interfund payable; enterprise fund reduction of a receivable
questions.exp: This is an interfund service provided and used (formerly a quasi-external transaction): it is reported as an expenditure or expense of the purchasing fund and revenue of the selling fund, as if with outsiders. Transfers apply only to nonreciprocal flows.

questions.q: In a government's statement of activities, how are property taxes levied for general purposes reported?
choices: As other financing sources
As a reduction of the expenses of each function
As program revenue of the general government function
As general revenues, reported after the net (expense) revenue of the functions
questions.exp: The statement of activities uses a net (expense) revenue format: program revenues (charges for services and program-specific grants) offset each function's expenses, and taxes, including those levied for specific purposes, are general revenues reported at the bottom. Calling them program revenue misreads the format.

questions.q: Other than the general fund, which is always major, what quantitative test must an individual governmental fund meet to be reported as a major fund?
choices: Its total assets plus deferred outflows, liabilities plus deferred inflows, revenues, or expenditures are at least 10% of the governmental funds total for that element and at least 5% of the combined governmental and enterprise funds total for the same element
It is designated as major by the auditor
Its fund balance is at least 5% of total governmental fund balances
Its total revenues exceed 10% of the government's total revenues
questions.exp: GASB 34 (as amended by GASB 65) requires the same element to meet both the 10% test (within its fund category) and the 5% test (governmental plus enterprise combined). A government may also choose to report any fund it considers important as major.

questions.q: For the year, the net change in a city's governmental fund balances was $500,000. During the year: capital outlay expenditures were $800,000; depreciation expense was $300,000; general obligation bonds were issued for $1,000,000; and bond principal repayments were $200,000. Assuming no other reconciling items, what is the change in net position of governmental activities?
questions.exp: $500,000 + $800,000 capital outlay - $300,000 depreciation - $1,000,000 bond proceeds + $200,000 principal repayments = $200,000. Bond proceeds increase fund balance but are a liability, not revenue, in the government-wide statements, so adding them ($2,200,000) is the trap.

questions.q: A city's governmental activities report capital assets, net of accumulated depreciation, of $10,000,000. Outstanding bonds attributable to acquiring those assets total $6,000,000, and all bond proceeds have been spent. The city also holds $500,000 of cash restricted for debt service. What should be reported as net investment in capital assets?
questions.exp: Net investment in capital assets = capital assets net of depreciation less outstanding debt attributable to them: $10,000,000 - $6,000,000 = $4,000,000 (GASB 63). The restricted debt service cash belongs in restricted net position, not net investment in capital assets.

questions.q: A city was awarded a $500,000 state grant that reimburses allowable costs incurred for a job-training program. During the year, the city incurred $320,000 of allowable costs and received $250,000 of reimbursements. What grant revenue should be reported in the government-wide statement of activities?
questions.exp: For a reimbursement-type grant, incurring allowable costs is an eligibility requirement, so revenue is recognized as qualifying costs are incurred (GASB 33): $320,000. Recognizing only the cash received confuses revenue with collection.

questions.q: Under GASB 33, when should a city recognize revenue from its local sales tax (a derived tax revenue) in the government-wide statements?
choices: When the city's budget is adopted
When the underlying sales transactions occur
When the tax rate is enacted
When the state remits the tax to the city
questions.exp: Derived tax revenues, such as sales and income taxes, are recognized when the underlying exchange transaction occurs (accrual basis); governmental funds also require that the resources be available. Recognition on remittance is a cash-basis approach.

questions.q: Under GASB 68, where is a city's net pension liability for its general government employees reported?
choices: In a pension trust fund as a liability of the employer
In the government-wide statement of net position (governmental activities), but not in the governmental fund balance sheet
In the general fund balance sheet
Only in the notes to the financial statements
questions.exp: The net pension liability is a long-term obligation reported under the economic resources focus in the government-wide statements (and in proprietary funds for their employees); governmental funds report only amounts due and payable from current resources. The pension trust fund reports the plan's own assets, not the employer's liability.

questions.q: On the first day of the fiscal year, a city's general fund entered into a 5-year lease of office equipment. The present value of the lease payments is $300,000. Under GASB 87, how should the general fund report the lease at commencement?
choices: A right-to-use asset and a lease liability of $300,000
Rent expense recognized straight-line over 5 years
An expenditure (capital outlay) and an other financing source of $300,000
Expenditures only as the lease payments are made
questions.exp: Under GASB 87, a governmental fund reports a lessee's lease at commencement as a capital outlay expenditure and an other financing source equal to the initial lease liability. The intangible right-to-use asset and lease liability appear in the government-wide statements.

questions.q: In the statement of cash flows of a city's enterprise fund, how should interest paid on revenue bonds issued to build a water treatment plant be classified?
choices: Investing activities
Noncapital financing activities
Capital and related financing activities
Operating activities
questions.exp: GASB 9 uses four categories for proprietary funds; interest and principal paid on debt issued to acquire capital assets are capital and related financing activities. Interest on debt not related to capital assets would be noncapital financing; in a business enterprise interest paid is operating.

questions.q: A state shares a portion of its gasoline tax with a city, and state law restricts its use to road maintenance. In which governmental fund would the city typically account for these resources?
choices: Permanent fund
Special revenue fund
Capital projects fund
Debt service fund
questions.exp: Special revenue funds account for specific revenue sources restricted or committed to specified purposes other than debt service or capital projects (GASB 54). Road maintenance is an operating purpose, not a capital project.

questions.q: A city's general fund uses the consumption method for supplies. Supplies inventory was $5,000 at the beginning of the year and $8,000 at the end, and supplies purchased during the year cost $40,000. What supplies expenditure should the general fund report?
questions.exp: Under the consumption method, expenditures equal supplies used: $5,000 + $40,000 - $8,000 = $37,000. $40,000 is the purchases method result.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a fiduciary fund type?
choices: Investment trust fund
Private-purpose trust fund
Custodial fund
Internal service fund
questions.exp: Internal service funds are proprietary funds that serve the government's own departments. Fiduciary funds are pension (and other employee benefit) trust, investment trust, private-purpose trust, and custodial funds (GASB 84).

questions.q: A company sells equipment, installation and a two-year service plan to a customer for a single price of $100,000. The standalone selling prices are equipment $80,000, installation $10,000 and service plan $30,000. Each is a distinct performance obligation. How much of the transaction price is allocated to the equipment?
questions.exp: ASC 606 allocates the transaction price on a relative standalone selling price basis: $100,000 x ($80,000 / $120,000) = $66,667. Allocating the full $80,000 standalone price ignores the $20,000 bundle discount, which is spread across all obligations.

questions.q: A contractor agrees to build a facility for $500,000 and will receive a $60,000 bonus if the facility is completed by a specified date. The contractor estimates a 70% probability of earning the bonus. Assume the variable consideration constraint does not limit the estimate. What transaction price should the contractor use?
questions.exp: With only two possible outcomes, the most likely amount method best predicts the consideration, so the bonus is included in full: $500,000 + $60,000 = $560,000. The expected value method ($500,000 + 70% x $60,000 = $542,000) is the trap; it suits contracts with many possible outcomes.

questions.q: A company with many similar contracts agrees to provide services for $50,000, subject to late-delivery penalties. Based on experience, it estimates a 50% chance of no penalty, a 30% chance of a $5,000 penalty and a 20% chance of a $10,000 penalty. Assume the constraint does not apply. Using the method that best predicts the consideration, what is the transaction price?
questions.exp: With a range of outcomes and many similar contracts, the expected value method is appropriate: expected penalty = (30% x $5,000) + (20% x $10,000) = $3,500, so the price is $50,000 - $3,500 = $46,500. Using the most likely outcome of no penalty gives the $50,000 trap.

questions.q: A retailer sells 1,000 units at $50 each (cost $30 each) with a right of return. Based on reliable experience, it expects 5% of units to be returned. How much revenue should the retailer recognize at the time of sale?
questions.exp: Under ASC 606, revenue excludes expected returns: 950 units x $50 = $47,500, with a $2,500 refund liability and a $1,500 asset for the right to recover goods (50 x $30). Recognizing the full $50,000 ignores the variable consideration from returns.

questions.q: An online travel company collects $200 from a customer for a hotel room and remits $170 to the hotel. The travel company never controls the room, and the hotel is responsible for providing it. How much revenue should the travel company recognize?
choices: $0, because no service is performed
questions.exp: Because the company does not control the room before it is transferred, it is an agent and recognizes revenue net, equal to its $30 commission (ASC 606-10-55-36 through 55-40). Reporting $200 gross is the principal treatment, which does not apply here.

questions.q: A contractor has a $3,000,000 fixed-price contract and recognizes revenue over time using the cost-to-cost input method. In Year 1, it incurred costs of $600,000 and estimates additional costs to complete of $1,800,000. How much revenue should it recognize in Year 1?
questions.exp: Progress = $600,000 / ($600,000 + $1,800,000) = 25%, so revenue = 25% x $3,000,000 = $750,000. Dividing costs incurred by only the remaining costs ($600,000 / $1,800,000) produces the $1,000,000 trap, and $150,000 is the gross profit.
