questions.q: A contractor has a $2,000,000 fixed-price contract recognized over time. At the end of Year 1, costs incurred are $900,000 and estimated costs to complete are $1,300,000. What loss should the contractor recognize on the contract in Year 1?
questions.exp: Total estimated cost of $2,200,000 exceeds the $2,000,000 price, and the entire expected loss of $200,000 must be recognized as soon as it is anticipated (ASC 605-35). Recognizing only the portion tied to progress ($900,000 / $2,200,000 x $200,000 = $81,818) is the trap.

questions.q: On January 1, Year 1, a company delivers equipment to a customer who will pay $121,000 on December 31, Year 2. The cash selling price of the equipment is $100,000, reflecting a 10% annual financing rate. Control transfers on delivery. How much revenue from the sale of equipment is recognized on January 1, Year 1?
choices: $0 until cash is collected
questions.exp: A significant financing component exists, so revenue is recognized at the cash selling price of $100,000 and the $21,000 difference is interest income over two years ($10,000 in Year 1). Recognizing $121,000 ignores the financing component.

questions.q: A company paid a $20,000 commission to a salesperson for signing a four-year service contract, paid $3,000 in travel costs to make the sales pitch, and incurred $2,000 of legal fees to draft the contract that would have been incurred even if the contract had not been signed. How much should be capitalized as an incremental cost of obtaining the contract?
questions.exp: Under ASC 340-40, only costs incurred because the contract was obtained, such as the $20,000 commission, are capitalized and amortized over the four-year term. Travel and legal costs incurred regardless of whether the contract is obtained are expensed, so $25,000 overstates the asset.

questions.q: A manufacturer sells appliances with a standard 90-day warranty that the products will work as specified, and customers may also buy a separately priced three-year extended warranty. How should the two warranties be accounted for?
choices: Both are separate performance obligations with revenue deferred
Both are accrued as warranty expense with no revenue deferral
The standard warranty is accrued as a cost under ASC 460 and the extended warranty is a separate performance obligation
The extended warranty is accrued as an expense and the standard warranty is a performance obligation
questions.exp: An assurance-type warranty that only promises the product meets specifications is accrued as a cost, while a warranty the customer can buy separately is a service-type warranty and a distinct performance obligation (ASC 606-10-55-30 through 55-35). Treating both as expense accruals is the most common error.

questions.q: On January 1, a company sells a machine bundled with a three-year extended service-type warranty for $1,080. Standalone selling prices are $1,000 for the machine and $200 for the warranty. Warranty revenue is recognized straight-line from the date of sale. How much revenue should the company recognize in the year of sale?
questions.exp: Warranty allocation = $1,080 x $200 / $1,200 = $180 and machine = $900; revenue in Year 1 = $900 + ($180 / 3) = $960. Recognizing the entire $1,080 at sale ignores that the warranty is satisfied over time.

questions.q: A company grants a franchisee the right to use its trade name and brand for 10 years in exchange for an upfront fee. The company will continue activities that significantly affect the brand. How should the upfront fee be recognized?
choices: When cash is received
Over time over the license term, because it is a right to access symbolic intellectual property
Only at the end of the license term
At the point in time the license is granted, because it is a right to use functional intellectual property
questions.exp: A brand or trade name is symbolic IP, and a license to it is a right to access recognized over time (ASC 606-10-55-58 through 55-63). Point-in-time recognition applies to functional IP such as completed software or film.

questions.q: A software company licenses functional IP and receives a royalty equal to 5% of the licensee's sales of products incorporating the software. How should the company recognize the royalty revenue?
choices: Recognize royalties only when cash is received
Recognize royalties at the later of when the licensee's sales occur or the related performance obligation is satisfied
Recognize royalties evenly over the contract term
Estimate total royalties and recognize them when the license is transferred
questions.exp: The sales- or usage-based royalty exception in ASC 606-10-55-65 prohibits estimating these royalties up front; they are recognized at the later of the subsequent sale or satisfaction of the obligation. Estimating total royalties under the general variable consideration guidance is the trap.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the criteria that must be met for a seller to recognize revenue in a bill-and-hold arrangement?
choices: The reason for the arrangement is substantive
The product is ready for physical transfer to the customer
The product is identified separately as belonging to the customer
The customer has paid the full purchase price in advance
questions.exp: ASC 606-10-55-83 requires a substantive reason, separate identification, readiness for physical transfer, and that the seller cannot use the product or direct it to another customer. Payment in advance is not a requirement.

questions.q: A consignor shipped goods costing $60,000 to a consignee. During the year, the consignee sold 40% of the goods to end customers for $50,000 and kept a 10% commission. The consignor is the principal. How much revenue should the consignor recognize?
questions.exp: A consignor recognizes revenue only when goods are sold to end customers, and as principal it reports the gross sales of $50,000 with a $5,000 commission expense. Reporting $45,000 nets the commission against revenue, which is incorrect for a principal.

questions.q: A retailer sold $100,000 of gift cards during the year and expects 10% to never be redeemed, based on reliable history. Customers redeemed $45,000 of gift cards during the year. Breakage is recognized in proportion to the pattern of redemption. How much revenue should the retailer recognize this year related to the gift cards?
questions.exp: Expected redemptions are $90,000; $45,000 redeemed is 50% of that, so 50% of expected breakage ($10,000) is recognized: $45,000 + $5,000 = $50,000 (ASC 606-10-55-48). Recognizing all $10,000 of breakage immediately gives the $55,000 trap.

questions.q: A retailer's sales were $100,000 this period, and customers earned 10,000 loyalty points, each redeemable for a $1 discount on future purchases. The retailer expects 80% of points to be redeemed. Points are a material right. How much revenue should be recognized on the sales this period?
questions.exp: The points' standalone selling price is $8,000 (10,000 x $1 x 80%), so revenue for goods = $100,000 x $100,000 / $108,000 = $92,593, and $7,407 is deferred. Subtracting the $8,000 directly ($92,000) skips the relative standalone selling price allocation.

questions.q: A beverage maker sold $200,000 of products to a grocery chain and paid the chain $10,000 in slotting fees for shelf space. The maker receives no distinct good or service in exchange for the fees. How much revenue should the beverage maker recognize?
choices: $200,000, with $10,000 recorded as a prepaid asset
$200,000, with $10,000 of selling expense
questions.exp: Consideration payable to a customer that is not for a distinct good or service reduces the transaction price (ASC 606-10-32-25), so revenue is $190,000. Recording it as selling expense with $200,000 of revenue is the trap.

questions.q: A contract calls for 120 distinct units at $100 each. After 60 units are delivered, the contract is modified to add 30 more units at $80 each, which is not the standalone selling price. The remaining goods are distinct from those already transferred. At what price per unit should revenue be recognized for the remaining 90 units?
choices: $100 for the original units and $80 for the added units
questions.exp: Because the added goods are not priced at standalone selling price but the remaining goods are distinct, the modification is treated as termination of the old contract and creation of a new one: (60 x $100 + 30 x $80) / 90 = $93.33. Keeping separate prices applies only when the added goods are priced at standalone selling price.

questions.q: Under ASC 606, when should an entity present a receivable rather than a contract asset for its right to consideration?
choices: When the entity has satisfied any performance obligation
When the right to consideration is unconditional, requiring only the passage of time
When an invoice has been prepared, regardless of remaining obligations
When the customer has signed the contract
questions.exp: A receivable is an unconditional right to consideration; if the right depends on something other than the passage of time, such as future performance, it is a contract asset. Satisfying one obligation while payment still depends on another produces a contract asset, not a receivable.

questions.q: Which situation would NOT, by itself, cause a performance obligation to be satisfied over time under ASC 606?
choices: The entity's performance creates an asset with no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date
The entity's performance creates an asset with an alternative use to the entity
The entity's performance creates an asset the customer controls as it is created
The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs
questions.exp: The third over-time criterion requires both no alternative use and an enforceable right to payment (ASC 606-10-25-27); an asset with an alternative use fails it. The other situations each satisfy one of the over-time criteria.

questions.q: During the year, a company classified a component as held for sale; the disposal represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations. The component had an operating loss of $300,000 for the year, and its carrying amount of $2,000,000 exceeds its fair value less cost to sell of $1,700,000. The tax rate is 25%. What amount should be reported as loss from discontinued operations, net of tax?
questions.exp: The operating loss and the $300,000 write-down to fair value less cost to sell are both reported in discontinued operations: ($300,000 + $300,000) x (1 - 25%) = $450,000 (ASC 205-20). Omitting the tax effect gives $600,000, and omitting the write-down gives $225,000.

questions.q: Which disposal is most likely to be reported as a discontinued operation under ASC 205-20?
choices: Sale of one of 40 retail stores in a region the company continues to serve
Discontinuing one minor product line within a product group
Sale of a major geographic segment that represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations and results
Sale of excess manufacturing equipment
questions.exp: A disposal qualifies only if it represents a strategic shift that has, or will have, a major effect on operations and financial results, such as exiting a major geographic area. Selling one store or a minor product line typically does not meet that threshold.

questions.q: How should a material gain that is both unusual in nature and infrequent in occurrence be presented on the income statement under current U.S. GAAP?
choices: As a separate line item within income from continuing operations, before tax
In other comprehensive income
As an adjustment to beginning retained earnings
As an extraordinary item, net of tax, after discontinued operations
questions.exp: ASU 2015-01 eliminated extraordinary items; unusual or infrequent items are reported separately within income from continuing operations on a pretax basis or disclosed in the notes (ASC 225-20). Net-of-tax extraordinary presentation is no longer permitted.

questions.q: A company had net income of $1,000,000. It has 10,000 shares of $100 par, 6% cumulative preferred stock outstanding; no dividends were declared this year. It had 200,000 common shares outstanding on January 1 and issued 60,000 common shares on July 1. What is basic earnings per share?
questions.exp: Cumulative preferred dividends are deducted whether or not declared: ($1,000,000 - $60,000) / (200,000 + 60,000 x 6/12) = $940,000 / 230,000 = $4.09 (ASC 260). Ignoring the undeclared preferred dividend gives $4.35.

questions.q: A company had 100,000 common shares outstanding on January 1. It issued 20,000 shares for cash on April 1 and distributed a 10% stock dividend on October 1. What is the weighted-average number of shares for basic EPS?
questions.exp: Stock dividends are applied retroactively to all shares outstanding before them: 100,000 x 1.10 + 20,000 x 1.10 x 9/12 = 110,000 + 16,500 = 126,500. Failing to restate the April issuance for the dividend gives 125,000.

questions.q: A company had net income of $500,000 and 100,000 common shares outstanding all year. It also had $1,000,000 of 6% bonds outstanding all year, convertible into 20,000 common shares. The tax rate is 25%. What is diluted earnings per share?
questions.exp: Under the if-converted method, add back after-tax interest of $60,000 x 75% = $45,000: ($500,000 + $45,000) / 120,000 = $4.54; the bonds are dilutive because $45,000 / 20,000 = $2.25 is below basic EPS of $5.00. Adding back pretax interest gives the $4.67 trap.

questions.q: A company changes from the double-declining-balance to the straight-line depreciation method for its existing equipment. How should this change be accounted for?
choices: Retrospectively, by restating prior periods
As a correction of an error
Prospectively, as a change in estimate effected by a change in accounting principle
As a cumulative-effect adjustment in current-period net income
questions.exp: ASC 250 treats a change in depreciation method as a change in accounting estimate effected by a change in principle, applied prospectively. Retrospective restatement is required for most other changes in principle, which is why it is the tempting choice.

questions.q: A company receives a $50,000 nonrefundable deposit from a customer under an agreement for which collectibility of the remaining consideration is not probable, so the contract does not meet the ASC 606 criteria. The company has not transferred goods and continues to have obligations under the agreement. How should the deposit be recorded?
choices: As deferred revenue recognized straight-line over the contract term
As revenue when received, because it is nonrefundable
As a liability until the contract criteria are met or another ASC 606 event allows revenue recognition
As a reduction of accounts receivable
questions.exp: When a contract fails the existence criteria, consideration received is a liability until the criteria are met, or the entity has no remaining obligations and has received substantially all consideration, or the contract is terminated (ASC 606-10-25-7 and 25-8). Being nonrefundable alone does not permit revenue recognition.

questions.q: A company sells equipment to a customer for $500,000 and holds a call right to repurchase the equipment in two years for $550,000. How should the company account for the transaction?
choices: As a financing arrangement, because the repurchase price exceeds the original selling price
As a sale with a right of return
As a sale with revenue of $500,000 recognized at delivery
As a lease, because the repurchase price exceeds the selling price
questions.exp: When the seller has a call right, the customer never obtains control, and a repurchase price at or above the original selling price makes it a financing arrangement (ASC 606-10-55-68). Lease treatment applies only if the repurchase price is below the original selling price.

questions.q: In its first year of operations, Arch Co. recorded book depreciation of $100,000 and tax depreciation of $160,000 on its equipment. There are no other differences, and the enacted tax rate for all years is 25%. What amount of deferred income tax expense should Arch report?
questions.exp: The $60,000 excess of tax over book depreciation is a taxable temporary difference that creates a deferred tax liability of $60,000 x 25% = $15,000. $40,000 and $25,000 apply the rate to each depreciation amount separately rather than to the difference.

questions.q: Bale Corp. reported pretax financial income of $800,000, which included $40,000 of municipal bond interest. Tax depreciation exceeded book depreciation by $60,000. The enacted tax rate is 25% for all years. What total income tax expense should Bale report?
questions.exp: Total expense = (pretax income - permanent differences) x rate = ($800,000 - $40,000) x 25% = $190,000, made up of current tax $175,000 ($700,000 x 25%) and deferred tax $15,000. $175,000 is only the current portion.

questions.q: At December 31, Year 1, Cole Co. had a $300,000 taxable temporary difference that will reverse equally in Years 2, 3, and 4. Enacted tax rates are 25% for Years 2 and 3 and 21% for Year 4; a bill proposing 19% for Year 4 has not been enacted. What deferred tax liability should Cole report at December 31, Year 1?
questions.exp: Deferred taxes are measured using enacted rates for the years in which the differences reverse (ASC 740-10-30-8): $100,000 x 25% + $100,000 x 25% + $100,000 x 21% = $71,000. Proposed but unenacted rates are ignored, so $69,000 (using 19%) is wrong.

questions.q: At year-end, Dyer Co. had gross deferred tax assets of $200,000. Based on the weight of available evidence, it is more likely than not that $60,000 of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. What net deferred tax asset should Dyer report?
questions.exp: A valuation allowance is recorded for the portion of deferred tax assets that is more likely than not (over 50%) to go unrealized: $200,000 - $60,000 = $140,000 (ASC 740-10-30-5). Writing off the whole asset applies a stricter threshold than the standard requires.

questions.q: Which of the following creates a deferred tax asset?
choices: Using an installment sale method for tax for a sale recognized in full for book
Taking accelerated depreciation for tax and straight-line for book
Deducting a prepaid expense for tax when paid while expensing it for book over the coverage period
Receiving rent in advance that is taxable when received but recognized for book when earned
questions.exp: Advance rent is taxed now but will be book income later, so future taxable income will be smaller; that future deductible amount is a deferred tax asset. The other three items defer taxable income or accelerate deductions, which creates deferred tax liabilities.

questions.q: In Year 1, Eads Co. accrued $50,000 of warranty expense for book purposes and paid $20,000 of warranty claims, which are deductible for tax only when paid. The enacted tax rate is 25% for all years. By how much should Eads's deferred tax asset increase in Year 1?
questions.exp: The unpaid accrual of $30,000 ($50,000 - $20,000) is a deductible temporary difference: $30,000 x 25% = $7,500. $12,500 applies the rate to the full accrual, but $20,000 has already been deducted on the tax return.

questions.q: Which of the following is a permanent difference rather than a temporary difference?
choices: Premiums on officers' life insurance for which the corporation is the beneficiary
Subscription revenue received in advance and taxed when received
Warranty costs accrued for book purposes but deducted for tax when paid
Depreciation computed using MACRS for tax and straight-line for book
questions.exp: Life insurance premiums where the company is the beneficiary are never deductible, and the proceeds are never taxable, so the difference never reverses and creates no deferred tax. The other items reverse over time and are temporary differences.

questions.q: In Year 1, Fane Co., a calendar-year C corporation, incurred a net operating loss of $400,000 for federal tax purposes. The enacted federal rate is 21%, and it is more likely than not that the full loss will be used against future taxable income. How should Fane account for the NOL in Year 1?
choices: Recognize a refund receivable of $84,000 from carrying the loss back two years
Recognize a deferred tax asset of $67,200, because carryforwards are limited to 80% of taxable income
Recognize a deferred tax asset and an income tax benefit of $84,000
Recognize no benefit until the loss is used
questions.exp: Federal NOLs arising after 2020 generally cannot be carried back but may be carried forward indefinitely, so the carryforward creates a deferred tax asset of $400,000 x 21% = $84,000, less any needed valuation allowance (ASC 740-10-25). The 80% of taxable income limit affects when the NOL is used, not the gross deferred tax asset.

questions.q: Gill Co. took a tax position worth a $100,000 tax benefit that is more likely than not to be sustained on examination. The estimated probabilities of the benefit realized on settlement are: $100,000 (30%), $80,000 (25%), $60,000 (25%), and $40,000 (20%). What tax benefit should Gill recognize?
questions.exp: Under ASC 740-10-30-7, the benefit recognized is the largest amount that is more than 50% likely to be realized. Cumulative probabilities are $100,000 at 30% and $80,000 at 55%, so recognize $80,000. Recognizing $100,000 ignores the measurement step that follows recognition.

questions.q: Hart Co. claimed a $50,000 tax benefit for a deduction on its tax return. Management concludes that the position is not more likely than not to be sustained on examination by the taxing authority, based on its technical merits. How should Hart account for the position?
choices: Recognize no benefit and record a $50,000 liability for the unrecognized tax benefit
Recognize the $50,000 benefit and disclose the uncertainty
Recognize 50% of the benefit
Recognize a benefit equal to the probability-weighted expected value
questions.exp: A position that fails the more-likely-than-not recognition threshold gets no benefit; the benefit claimed on the return is recorded as a liability for unrecognized tax benefits (ASC 740-10-25-6). Probability weighting is not used under ASC 740's two-step model.

questions.q: Ivey Co. had a deferred tax liability of $300,000, based on $1,000,000 of taxable temporary differences and a 30% rate. During the year, legislation was enacted lowering the rate to 21% for all future years. How should Ivey account for the change?
choices: Recognize the effect prospectively as the temporary differences reverse
Adjust beginning retained earnings by $90,000
Recognize a $90,000 deferred tax benefit in income from continuing operations in the period of enactment
Recognize a $90,000 gain in other comprehensive income
questions.exp: The effect of an enacted rate change on existing deferred tax balances is recognized in income from continuing operations in the period that includes the enactment date (ASC 740-10-35-4): DTL falls to $210,000, giving a $90,000 benefit. A retained earnings adjustment would treat it like an error correction.

questions.q: Joss Corp. had pretax income from continuing operations of $500,000 and a pretax loss from discontinued operations of $100,000. The tax rate is 25%. Under intraperiod tax allocation, what income tax expense should be reported in income from continuing operations?
questions.exp: Intraperiod allocation assigns tax to continuing operations first, on its own income: $500,000 x 25% = $125,000; the $25,000 benefit is allocated to discontinued operations, which is reported net at $75,000. $100,000 is total tax on combined income.

questions.q: At the end of Year 2, Kemp Co. had $240,000 of cumulative taxable temporary differences on equipment, and its deferred tax liability at the beginning of Year 2 was $45,000. Taxable income for Year 2 was $600,000. The enacted rate is 25% for all years, and there are no other differences. What total income tax expense should Kemp report for Year 2?
questions.exp: Current tax = $600,000 x 25% = $150,000. Ending DTL = $240,000 x 25% = $60,000, so deferred expense = $60,000 - $45,000 = $15,000; total = $165,000. $210,000 adds the entire ending DTL instead of the change in it.

questions.q: Lund Co., a public company, recorded $1,500,000 of goodwill in a taxable business combination; the tax basis of the goodwill is also $1,500,000. For tax purposes the goodwill is amortized over 15 years; for book purposes it is not amortized and is not impaired in Year 1. At a 25% rate, what deferred tax balance related to goodwill should Lund report at the end of Year 1?
choices: Deferred tax asset of $25,000
Deferred tax liability of $25,000
No deferred tax, because goodwill is excluded from deferred tax accounting
Deferred tax liability of $375,000
questions.exp: After Year 1, the book basis ($1,500,000) exceeds the tax basis ($1,400,000) by $100,000, a taxable temporary difference: $100,000 x 25% = $25,000 DTL. The exception that bars recognizing deferred taxes applies only to the excess of book goodwill over tax-deductible goodwill at acquisition.

questions.q: Mead Co.'s pretax income was $200,000 in Q1 and $250,000 in Q2. At the end of Q1, Mead estimated its annual effective tax rate at 24%; at the end of Q2 it revised the estimate to 26%. What income tax expense should Mead report for Q2?
questions.exp: Interim tax = year-to-date income x current estimated annual effective rate, less tax already reported (ASC 740-270): $450,000 x 26% = $117,000, less Q1's $48,000 = $69,000. $65,000 applies the new rate only to Q2 income and omits the catch-up on Q1.

questions.q: Nolan Co. has a deferred tax asset in the U.S. federal jurisdiction and a deferred tax liability in a foreign jurisdiction. How should these be presented on Nolan's balance sheet?
choices: Presented separately as a noncurrent asset and a noncurrent liability
Both omitted, because they offset
Netted into a single noncurrent amount
Netted into a single current amount
questions.exp: Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only within the same tax-paying component and jurisdiction (ASC 740-10-45-6). Balances in different jurisdictions are shown separately, all as noncurrent.

questions.q: In Year 1, Orr Co. sold land with a $300,000 gain, which it recognized in full for financial reporting. For tax purposes the sale qualifies for the installment method, and one-third of the proceeds were collected in Year 1. The enacted tax rate is 25%. What deferred tax liability should Orr report at the end of Year 1?
questions.exp: Two-thirds of the gain ($200,000) will be taxed in future years, creating a taxable temporary difference: $200,000 x 25% = $50,000. $75,000 applies the rate to the whole gain, but one-third has already been taxed.

questions.q: Pyle Co. holds equity securities with readily determinable fair values. During the year it recognized a $40,000 unrealized holding gain in net income; the gain is taxable only when the securities are sold. The tax rate is 25%. How should Pyle report the related deferred tax?
choices: Deferred tax liability of $10,000, with deferred tax expense in net income
Deferred tax liability of $10,000, recorded in other comprehensive income
Deferred tax asset of $10,000
No deferred tax, because the gain is unrealized
questions.exp: Since ASU 2016-01, changes in fair value of equity securities go to net income, so the $40,000 book-over-tax basis difference creates a $10,000 DTL whose tax effect is also in net income. OCI applies to AFS debt securities, not equity securities.

questions.q: Which of the following is the strongest positive evidence supporting the conclusion that no valuation allowance is needed for a deferred tax asset?
choices: Losses expected in early future years by a currently profitable entity
A history of operating loss carryforwards expiring unused
Cumulative losses in recent years
Existing contracts or a sales backlog that will produce enough taxable income to realize the asset
questions.exp: ASC 740-10-30-22 lists existing contracts or a firm sales backlog as positive evidence. The other three items are examples of negative evidence, and cumulative losses in recent years are especially hard to overcome.

questions.q: Quin Co. holds available-for-sale debt securities that increased in fair value by $80,000 during the year. The gain is taxable only when the securities are sold, and the tax rate is 25%. Where should the related $20,000 deferred tax expense be reported?
choices: It is not recognized until the securities are sold
In other comprehensive income, netted against the unrealized gain
As a direct reduction of retained earnings
In income tax expense in income from continuing operations
questions.exp: Under intraperiod tax allocation, the tax effect follows the item that caused it. The unrealized AFS gain is reported in OCI, so its $20,000 deferred tax is also charged to OCI and the gain appears net at $60,000. Charging it to continuing operations would mismatch the tax and the gain.

questions.q: On October 1, Rusk Co. paid a 12-month insurance premium of $48,000, which was deductible in full for tax in the year paid. For book purposes, $36,000 was reported as prepaid insurance at December 31. The tax rate is 25%. What deferred tax amount arises from the prepaid insurance at December 31?
choices: Deferred tax liability of $9,000
Deferred tax liability of $12,000
Deferred tax asset of $3,000
Deferred tax asset of $9,000
questions.exp: The prepaid asset has a $36,000 book basis and a zero tax basis, so future book expense will not be deductible: a taxable temporary difference creating a DTL of $36,000 x 25% = $9,000. A deferred tax asset reverses the direction of the difference.

questions.q: Sora Co. accrued a $200,000 litigation loss that will be deductible for tax purposes when paid, which is expected in two years. The enacted federal rate is 21%, and realization of deferred tax assets is more likely than not. What should Sora record related to the accrual?
choices: A current tax receivable of $42,000
No deferred tax, because the loss is contingent
A deferred tax liability of $42,000
A deferred tax asset of $42,000
questions.exp: The accrued liability has a book basis of $200,000 and a tax basis of zero, producing future deductions: a deductible temporary difference and a deferred tax asset of $200,000 x 21% = $42,000. Nothing is currently refundable, so a receivable is wrong.

questions.q: When employees exercise stock options, Tobin Co. receives a tax deduction that exceeds the cumulative book compensation cost recognized for the awards. Under current GAAP, how should Tobin recognize the excess tax benefit?
choices: As a deferred tax asset to be realized in future years
As a credit to additional paid-in capital
As a reduction of goodwill
As a reduction of income tax expense in the income statement
questions.exp: ASU 2016-09 requires all excess tax benefits and tax deficiencies on share-based payments to be recognized in income tax expense in the period they arise. Crediting APIC (the APIC pool approach) was eliminated.

questions.q: Ulm Corp. received $100,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 10%; the dividends are included in its $1,000,000 of pretax financial income. The dividends qualify for a 50% dividends-received deduction, and there are no other differences. At a 21% federal rate, what is Ulm's current federal income tax expense?
questions.exp: The DRD is a permanent difference: taxable income = $1,000,000 - $50,000 = $950,000, x 21% = $199,500. $195,300 uses the 70% DRD that applied to less-than-20%-owned corporations before the TCJA.

questions.q: On December 15, Year 1, Congress was debating a bill that would lower the corporate rate from 21% to 18% for Year 2 and later. The bill had not been enacted when Vance Co. issued its Year 1 financial statements. What rate should Vance use to measure deferred taxes at December 31, Year 1?
choices: 18%, because it is expected to apply when the differences reverse
21%, the enacted rate
18% for deferred tax liabilities and 21% for deferred tax assets
A probability-weighted blend of 21% and 18%
questions.exp: ASC 740 measures deferred taxes using enacted tax law and rates; expected or proposed changes are not anticipated. The effect of a change is recognized only in the period of enactment.

questions.q: In a nontaxable business combination, the fair value assigned to the acquiree's identifiable assets exceeds their carryover tax basis by $400,000. The enacted rate is 25%. What is the effect on the acquisition accounting?
choices: No deferred tax is recognized, because the basis differences arose in an acquisition
A $100,000 deferred tax liability is recognized, increasing goodwill by $100,000
A $100,000 deferred tax liability is recognized in income tax expense
A $100,000 deferred tax asset is recognized, reducing goodwill
questions.exp: ASC 805-740 requires deferred taxes for differences between assigned values and tax bases of the identifiable assets acquired. The $100,000 DTL reduces net identifiable assets and so increases goodwill; it does not hit income tax expense at acquisition.

questions.q: How may a company classify interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits in its income statement?
choices: As income tax expense or as interest/other expense, based on an accounting policy election applied consistently
Both must be charged directly to retained earnings
Interest must be classified as income tax expense; penalties as operating expense
Both must be classified as income tax expense
questions.exp: ASC 740-10-45-25 allows a policy election to classify interest as income tax expense or interest expense, and penalties as income tax expense or another expense, applied consistently and disclosed. Neither classification is mandatory.

questions.q: Wolfe Co. reported an allowance for uncollectible accounts of $80,000 at year-end. Bad debts are deductible for tax only when written off (direct write-off method), and the enacted tax rate is 25%. What deferred tax amount arises from the allowance?
choices: Deferred tax liability of $20,000
No deferred tax, because bad debts are a permanent difference
Deferred tax asset of $20,000
Deferred tax asset of $16,800
questions.exp: The receivable's tax basis exceeds its book basis by the $80,000 allowance, which will be deducted when written off: a deductible temporary difference and DTA of $80,000 x 25% = $20,000. A DTL would arise only if book basis exceeded tax basis.

questions.q: At the end of Year 1, Xeno Co. had a $120,000 valuation allowance against deferred tax assets from prior operating losses. Because of sustained profitability during Year 2, management now judges that all of the deferred tax assets are more likely than not to be realized in future years. How should Xeno account for eliminating the allowance in Year 2?
choices: As a $120,000 credit to other comprehensive income
As a $120,000 deferred tax benefit in income from continuing operations
As a $120,000 increase in beginning retained earnings
It should be released ratably as the deferred tax assets are realized
questions.exp: A change in judgment about the realizability of beginning-of-year deferred tax assets is a change in estimate, recognized in income from continuing operations in the period of the change (ASC 740-10-45-20). Adjusting retained earnings would treat it like an error correction.

questions.q: Parent paid $1,000,000 cash to acquire 100% of Target. Target's identifiable assets had a fair value of $1,200,000 and a carrying amount of $900,000, and its liabilities had a fair value and carrying amount of $400,000. How much goodwill should Parent recognize?
questions.exp: Goodwill = consideration of $1,000,000 - fair value of net identifiable assets ($1,200,000 - $400,000 = $800,000) = $200,000 (ASC 805-30-30-1). Using carrying amounts ($500,000 net) gives the $400,000 trap.

questions.q: An acquirer paid $700,000 for 100% of a business whose identifiable net assets have a fair value of $800,000. After reassessing that all assets and liabilities were correctly identified and measured, how should the acquirer account for the difference?
choices: Reduce the recorded amounts of noncurrent assets proportionately
Recognize a $100,000 credit to additional paid-in capital
Recognize negative goodwill as a liability
Recognize a $100,000 gain in earnings on the acquisition date
questions.exp: ASC 805-30-25-2 requires a bargain purchase gain in earnings after the acquirer reassesses its identification and measurement. Proportionately reducing noncurrent assets was the superseded pre-2009 approach.

questions.q: A reporting unit has a carrying amount of $2,300,000, including $500,000 of goodwill, and a fair value of $2,000,000. Under current U.S. GAAP for public business entities, what goodwill impairment loss should be recognized?
questions.exp: Under ASU 2017-04, the impairment loss is the excess of the reporting unit's carrying amount over its fair value, $2,300,000 - $2,000,000 = $300,000, limited to the goodwill balance (ASC 350-20-35-8). Writing off all goodwill confuses the cap with the loss.

questions.q: A reporting unit's fair value is $1,000,000. Its carrying amount is $1,800,000, of which $500,000 is goodwill. What goodwill impairment loss should be recognized?
questions.exp: The shortfall of $800,000 exceeds the goodwill balance, so the loss is limited to the $500,000 of goodwill allocated to the reporting unit (ASC 350-20-35-8). Recognizing $800,000 ignores the limit; other assets are tested under their own guidance.

questions.q: An entity elects to perform the optional qualitative assessment for goodwill impairment and concludes it is not more likely than not that a reporting unit's fair value is less than its carrying amount. What must it do next?
choices: Measure the implied fair value of goodwill
Nothing further is required for that reporting unit this year
Test the goodwill for recoverability using undiscounted cash flows
Perform the quantitative impairment test to confirm the conclusion
questions.exp: Under ASC 350-20-35-3A, if the qualitative assessment shows impairment is not more likely than not, the quantitative test is unnecessary. Implied fair value of goodwill was the eliminated Step 2, and undiscounted cash flows are used for long-lived assets, not goodwill.

questions.q: A private company elects the private company accounting alternative for goodwill. Which of the following describes its accounting?
choices: Goodwill is amortized over 40 years and never tested for impairment
Goodwill is expensed immediately at acquisition
Goodwill is amortized on a straight-line basis over 10 years, or less if more appropriate, and tested for impairment only when a triggering event occurs
Goodwill is not amortized but is tested annually for impairment at the reporting unit level
questions.exp: ASC 350-20-35-63 permits private companies to amortize goodwill straight-line over 10 years or less and to test for impairment only upon a triggering event, at the entity or reporting unit level. Annual testing without amortization is the public-entity model.

questions.q: On January 1, Year 1, a company purchased a patent for $170,000. The patent had a remaining legal life of 17 years and an estimated useful life of 10 years. On January 1, Year 4, the company paid $21,000 in legal fees to successfully defend the patent. What patent amortization expense should be recognized in Year 4?
questions.exp: Annual amortization is $170,000 / 10 = $17,000; the successful defense costs are capitalized and amortized over the remaining 7 years of useful life, $3,000 per year, for a total of $20,000. Expensing the legal fees in Year 4 gives $38,000, and using the 17-year legal life ($10,000 + $1,500 = $11,500) is wrong when useful life is shorter.

questions.q: A company incurred $60,000 of legal fees in an unsuccessful defense of a patent, after which the patent was determined to have no remaining value. The patent's carrying amount was $90,000. What total expense or loss should be recognized?
choices: $0, with the legal fees capitalized
questions.exp: Legal costs of an unsuccessful defense are expensed, and the worthless patent's $90,000 carrying amount is written off: $60,000 + $90,000 = $150,000. Capitalizing legal fees is appropriate only for a successful defense.

questions.q: A company spent $400,000 on research and development that resulted in a new product, then paid $20,000 in patent registration fees and $15,000 in legal fees to file the patent application. What amount should be capitalized as a patent?
questions.exp: R&D costs are expensed as incurred under ASC 730, so only the legal and registration costs of obtaining the internally developed patent, $35,000, are capitalized. Capitalizing the R&D gives $435,000.

questions.q: A software company developing a product for sale incurred: $300,000 for design and coding before technological feasibility; $120,000 for testing after technological feasibility; $80,000 to produce product masters; and $30,000 to duplicate software and package units for sale. What amount should be capitalized as software development costs?
questions.exp: Under ASC 985-20, costs after technological feasibility through product masters are capitalized: $120,000 + $80,000 = $200,000. Pre-feasibility costs are R&D expense, and duplication and packaging costs are inventory, so including them gives $230,000.

questions.q: A company has $600,000 of capitalized software development costs for a product with a remaining estimated economic life of five years. Current-year revenue from the product is $400,000, and total current and anticipated future revenue is $1,600,000. What is amortization expense for the current year?
questions.exp: ASC 985-20-35-1 requires the greater of the revenue-ratio amount ($600,000 x $400,000 / $1,600,000 = $150,000) or straight-line ($600,000 / 5 = $120,000). Using straight-line only gives the $120,000 trap.

questions.q: A company developed software for internal use and incurred: preliminary project stage evaluation $50,000; coding and installation $300,000; testing during development $40,000; data conversion $20,000; and employee training $25,000. How much should be capitalized under ASC 350-40?
questions.exp: Only application development stage costs are capitalized: coding and installation plus testing = $340,000. Preliminary project costs, training and data conversion (other than software developed for conversion) are expensed; including data conversion gives $360,000.

questions.q: A company enters into a cloud computing arrangement that is a service contract and incurs implementation costs during the application development stage. How should those costs be accounted for?
choices: Capitalized as an intangible asset and amortized over five years in all cases
Expensed as incurred because the company does not own the software
Capitalized and expensed over the term of the hosting arrangement, presented in the same income statement line as the hosting fees
Capitalized as property, plant and equipment
questions.exp: ASU 2018-15 (ASC 350-40) requires implementation costs of a hosting arrangement that is a service contract to be capitalized following the internal-use software stages and expensed over the arrangement's term, in the same line as the service fees. Expensing all such costs immediately is the trap.

questions.q: A company's trademark has an indefinite useful life and a carrying amount of $800,000. Its fair value is $650,000, and the undiscounted future cash flows it is expected to generate total $900,000. What impairment loss should be recognized?
choices: $0, because undiscounted cash flows exceed carrying amount
questions.exp: Indefinite-lived intangibles other than goodwill are tested by comparing fair value with carrying amount, with no undiscounted cash flow recoverability step (ASC 350-30-35-19): $800,000 - $650,000 = $150,000. Applying the ASC 360 recoverability test is the trap.

questions.q: A finite-lived customer list has a carrying amount of $400,000. Because a major customer was lost, the company tested it: undiscounted expected cash flows are $380,000 and fair value is $300,000. What impairment loss should be recognized?
questions.exp: Finite-lived intangibles follow ASC 360: the asset fails recoverability ($380,000 < $400,000), and the loss is carrying amount less fair value, $100,000. Measuring the loss against undiscounted cash flows gives $20,000.

questions.q: A company acquired a trademark whose registration can be renewed every 10 years at nominal cost. The company intends to renew indefinitely and has the ability to do so, and cash flows are expected to continue indefinitely. How should the trademark be accounted for?
choices: Amortized over the 10-year registration period
Amortized over 40 years
Expensed when acquired
Not amortized; tested for impairment at least annually
questions.exp: An intangible with an indefinite useful life is not amortized but is tested for impairment at least annually (ASC 350-30-35-15). Amortizing over the 10-year legal term ignores the renewal intent and ability.

questions.q: In a business combination, the acquirer obtains an in-process research and development project with a fair value of $2,000,000. How should the acquirer account for it at the acquisition date?
choices: Recognize it as an indefinite-lived intangible asset until the project is completed or abandoned
Expense it immediately as R&D
Recognize it as a finite-lived intangible and amortize it over five years
Include it in goodwill
questions.exp: ASC 805 and ASC 350-30-35-17A require acquired IPR&D in a business combination to be recognized at fair value as an indefinite-lived intangible until completion (then amortized) or abandonment (then written off). Immediate expensing applies to IPR&D acquired in an asset acquisition without alternative future use.

questions.q: During the year, a company incurred $200,000 of research salaries and $50,000 of materials used in research. It bought equipment for $300,000 with alternative future uses and a five-year life (straight-line), and equipment for $80,000 usable only on a single research project. It also performed $40,000 of research for a client under contract. What R&D expense should it report?
questions.exp: R&D expense = $200,000 + $50,000 + $60,000 depreciation on the alternative-use equipment + $80,000 for the single-project equipment = $390,000 (ASC 730-10-25-2). Research performed for others under contract is not the company's R&D, so including it gives $430,000.

questions.q: Which of the following activities is considered research and development under ASC 730?
choices: Routine quality control testing during commercial production
Design, construction and testing of preproduction prototypes
Seasonal design changes to existing products
Market research for a new product
questions.exp: ASC 730-10-55-1 lists design, construction and testing of preproduction prototypes as R&D. Routine quality control, market research and routine or seasonal design changes are specifically excluded.

questions.q: A newly formed corporation incurred $10,000 of legal fees to incorporate, $20,000 to train employees before opening a new store and $50,000 to purchase store equipment. How much should be expensed as start-up and organization costs?
questions.exp: ASC 720-15 requires start-up activities, including organization costs and preopening training, to be expensed as incurred: $10,000 + $20,000 = $30,000. Equipment is capitalized as PP&E; capitalizing organization costs is a tax concept (IRC Section 248), not GAAP.

questions.q: A franchisee paid a $100,000 initial fee for a 10-year franchise and pays continuing fees of 4% of sales. How should these costs be accounted for?
choices: Capitalize the initial fee and amortize it over 10 years; expense continuing fees as incurred
Expense both the initial fee and the continuing fees as incurred
Capitalize the initial fee as an indefinite-lived intangible and the continuing fees as prepaid assets
Capitalize the initial fee and the estimated total continuing fees
questions.exp: The initial franchise fee is an intangible asset amortized over the 10-year franchise term, while continuing fees relate to current-period sales and are expensed. A franchise with a fixed term is not indefinite-lived.

questions.q: When must goodwill of a public business entity be tested for impairment?
choices: Only when the entity's market capitalization falls below book value
Every three years at the entity level
At least annually at the reporting unit level, and between annual tests if a triggering event occurs
Only when a triggering event occurs
questions.exp: ASC 350-20-35-28 and 35-30 require testing at least annually at the reporting unit level and between annual tests when events indicate impairment is more likely than not. Testing only upon a triggering event is the private company alternative.

questions.q: A company is selling a business within a reporting unit. The business being sold has a fair value of $300,000, the portion of the reporting unit being retained has a fair value of $900,000, and the reporting unit's goodwill is $400,000. How much goodwill should be included in the carrying amount of the business sold?
questions.exp: ASC 350-20-40-3 allocates goodwill based on relative fair values: $400,000 x $300,000 / $1,200,000 = $100,000. Dividing by the retained portion only ($300,000 / $900,000) gives $133,333.

questions.q: A company paid $1,100,000 plus $50,000 of transaction costs to acquire a building (fair value $600,000) and a patent (fair value $400,000) in a transaction that is an asset acquisition, not a business combination. At what amount should the patent be recorded?
questions.exp: In an asset acquisition, cost including transaction costs ($1,150,000) is allocated by relative fair value and no goodwill is recognized (ASC 805-50-30): $1,150,000 x 40% = $460,000. Excluding transaction costs gives $440,000, and recording at fair value with the excess as goodwill applies business combination accounting.

questions.q: An acquirer incurred $250,000 of legal, accounting and advisory fees in completing a business combination. How should these costs be accounted for?
choices: Allocated to the identifiable assets acquired
Deducted from the fair value of the consideration transferred
Expensed in the periods the costs are incurred and services are received
Added to goodwill
questions.exp: ASC 805-10-25-23 requires acquisition-related costs to be expensed as incurred, except costs to issue debt or equity securities. Adding them to goodwill was the pre-2009 purchase method treatment.

questions.q: In a business combination, the acquiree's skilled, assembled workforce is estimated to be worth $500,000. How should the acquirer account for it?
choices: Recognize it as a separate finite-lived intangible asset
Recognize it as a separate indefinite-lived intangible asset
Do not recognize it separately; it is subsumed into goodwill
Expense it immediately
questions.exp: ASC 805-20-55-6 prohibits recognizing an assembled workforce as an identifiable intangible asset because it is neither separable nor contractual-legal; its value is included in goodwill. Recognizing it separately is the most tempting error.

questions.q: An acquirer paid $900,000 cash for 100% of a business and agreed to pay additional consideration if earnings targets are met; the contingent consideration's acquisition-date fair value is $100,000. The fair value of identifiable net assets is $850,000. What goodwill should be recognized?
questions.exp: Contingent consideration is included at acquisition-date fair value: ($900,000 + $100,000) - $850,000 = $150,000. Ignoring it until paid gives $50,000; later changes in the fair value of a contingent consideration liability go to earnings, not goodwill.

questions.q: A company paid $500,000 for a 10-year license. A third party has committed to purchase the license at the end of the 10 years for $100,000. What annual amortization should be recognized?
questions.exp: Residual value is recognized because a third party has committed to buy the asset (ASC 350-30-35-8): ($500,000 - $100,000) / 10 = $40,000. Assuming zero residual value, the general default, gives $50,000.

questions.q: A company determines that a trademark previously assessed as having an indefinite life now has a remaining useful life of five years. What should the company do?
choices: Test the trademark for impairment, then amortize its carrying amount prospectively over five years
Amortize the trademark retrospectively from acquisition
Continue not amortizing it but test it twice a year
Write the trademark off immediately
questions.exp: ASC 350-30-35-17 requires an impairment test when an indefinite-lived intangible is determined to have a finite life, followed by prospective amortization over the remaining useful life. Retrospective amortization would treat a change in estimate as an error.

questions.q: Nine months after a business combination, an acquirer obtains information about facts that existed at the acquisition date showing that the fair value of an acquired building was $450,000 rather than the provisional $500,000. How should the acquirer account for this?
choices: Restate prior-period financial statements as an error correction
Make no adjustment because the acquisition date has passed
Recognize a $50,000 impairment loss in the current period
Adjust the provisional amounts, increasing goodwill by $50,000, and recognize any related depreciation effect in the current period
questions.exp: Measurement-period adjustments within one year for facts existing at the acquisition date adjust the provisional amounts with an offset to goodwill, and the cumulative income effect is recorded in the current period (ASC 805-10-25-13 through 25-17). Prior periods are not restated after ASU 2015-16.

questions.q: A company using a periodic system had beginning inventory of 100 units at $10, then purchased 200 units at $12 and later 100 units at $15. It sold 250 units during the year. What is ending inventory under FIFO?
questions.exp: Under FIFO, the 150 units on hand are the most recent: 100 x $15 + 50 x $12 = $2,100. Periodic LIFO gives $1,600 (100 x $10 + 50 x $12), and weighted average gives $1,837.50.

questions.q: A company uses perpetual LIFO. It began the year with 200 units at $20, purchased 300 units at $22 on March 1, sold 400 units on April 1, and purchased 200 units at $25 on July 1. What is ending inventory?
questions.exp: The April sale takes 300 units at $22 and 100 at $20, leaving 100 at $20; adding the July purchase gives 100 x $20 + 200 x $25 = $7,000. Periodic LIFO, which assigns the year's latest costs to all sales, gives $6,200.

questions.q: A company uses the moving-average method in a perpetual system. It began with 100 units costing $1,000, purchased 100 units at $14, sold 150 units, then purchased 150 units at $16. What is ending inventory?
questions.exp: After the first purchase, 200 units cost $2,400 ($12 each); the sale leaves 50 units at $600; adding $2,400 gives 200 units costing $3,000. Periodic weighted average ($4,800 / 350 x 200 = $2,743) ignores the timing of the sale.

questions.q: A company uses FIFO and applies the lower of cost and net realizable value item by item. Item X has cost $20,000, NRV $18,000 and replacement cost $17,000. Item Y has cost $30,000, NRV $35,000 and replacement cost $28,000. At what amount should inventory be reported?
questions.exp: Under ASC 330-10-35-1B, FIFO inventory is measured at the lower of cost and NRV: X at $18,000 and Y at $30,000, for $48,000. Replacement cost is irrelevant for FIFO, so $45,000 (using replacement cost) is a trap, and $50,000 applies the test to total inventory.

questions.q: A company uses LIFO. An inventory item has a cost of $100, replacement cost of $70, selling price of $120, costs to sell of $20 and a normal profit margin of $36. At what amount should the item be reported?
questions.exp: LIFO inventory uses lower of cost or market; market is replacement cost limited by a ceiling of NRV ($120 - $20 = $100) and a floor of NRV less normal profit ($100 - $36 = $64). Replacement cost of $70 falls between them, and it is lower than the $100 cost.

questions.q: A company adopted dollar-value LIFO when its inventory was $100,000 at base-year prices. At the end of Year 1, inventory at year-end prices was $132,000 and the price index was 1.10. What is the dollar-value LIFO ending inventory for Year 1?
questions.exp: Base-year equivalent = $132,000 / 1.10 = $120,000, a $20,000 real increase; the new layer is costed at $20,000 x 1.10 = $22,000, so inventory = $100,000 + $22,000 = $122,000. Stopping at the $120,000 base-year amount omits pricing the new layer.

questions.q: A dollar-value LIFO company's layers are: base layer $100,000 (index 1.00) and a Year 1 layer of $20,000 at base prices (index 1.10). At the end of Year 2, inventory at current prices is $126,500 and the index is 1.15. What is Year 2 dollar-value LIFO inventory?
questions.exp: Year 2 base-year equivalent = $126,500 / 1.15 = $110,000, a $10,000 decrease that liquidates part of the Year 1 layer: $100,000 + $10,000 x 1.10 = $111,000. Pricing the remaining layer at the current 1.15 index gives the $111,500 trap.

questions.q: Using the conventional retail inventory method, a store had beginning inventory at cost $40,000 and retail $60,000; purchases at cost $160,000 and retail $240,000; freight-in $4,000; net markups $20,000; net markdowns $10,000; and sales $250,000. What is estimated ending inventory at cost?
questions.exp: The conventional method excludes markdowns from the ratio: $204,000 / $320,000 = 63.75%; ending retail = $320,000 - $10,000 - $250,000 = $60,000; cost = $38,250. Including markdowns in the denominator gives $39,484, the average-cost retail result.

questions.q: A fire destroyed a company's entire inventory. Beginning inventory was $80,000, purchases to the date of the fire were $300,000 and sales were $400,000. The company's gross profit is 30% of sales. What is the estimated cost of inventory destroyed?
questions.exp: Estimated COGS = $400,000 x 70% = $280,000; ending inventory = $80,000 + $300,000 - $280,000 = $100,000. Treating 30% as a markup on cost gives $72,308.

questions.q: A company overstated its ending inventory for Year 1 by $10,000. The error was not corrected. What is the effect on Year 2 net income and on retained earnings at the end of Year 2?
choices: Year 2 net income understated; retained earnings correct
Year 2 net income overstated; retained earnings overstated
Year 2 net income correct; retained earnings overstated
Year 2 net income understated; retained earnings understated
questions.exp: Overstated Year 1 ending inventory overstates Year 2 beginning inventory and COGS, understating Year 2 income by $10,000 and offsetting the Year 1 overstatement, so retained earnings at the end of Year 2 is correct. The error self-corrects over two years.

questions.q: A company's year-end physical count, taken in its warehouse, totaled $200,000. Not included were $15,000 of goods purchased FOB shipping point that were in transit and $8,000 (at cost) of goods sold FOB destination that were in transit to a customer. Included in the count were $12,000 of goods held on consignment for another company. What is the correct inventory?
questions.exp: Inventory = $200,000 + $15,000 (title passed at shipment) + $8,000 (title passes at destination, so seller still owns it) - $12,000 (consigned goods belong to the consignor) = $211,000. Forgetting the goods sold FOB destination gives $203,000.

questions.q: A company has a noncancelable, unhedged commitment to purchase 10,000 units at $20 per unit next year. At year-end, the market price has fallen to $17 per unit and the decline is expected to be permanent. What should the company report?
choices: A $200,000 liability for the full commitment
A $30,000 loss when the goods are received next year
Disclosure only, because no goods have been received
A $30,000 loss and liability at year-end
questions.exp: ASC 330-10-35-17 requires recognizing net losses on firm, noncancelable purchase commitments: 10,000 x ($20 - $17) = $30,000. Waiting until delivery or disclosing only fails to recognize a loss that already exists.

questions.q: A company purchased merchandise for $100,000 and paid freight-in of $5,000 and insurance in transit of $1,000. It took purchase discounts of $2,000, incurred $3,000 to store finished goods awaiting sale, and incurred $4,000 of abnormal spoilage. What is the cost of inventory?
questions.exp: Inventory cost = $100,000 + $5,000 + $1,000 - $2,000 = $104,000. Storage of finished goods and abnormal spoilage are period costs under ASC 330-10-30-7, so including storage gives $107,000.

questions.q: A manufacturer's fixed production overhead is $600,000. Normal capacity is 100,000 units, but actual production was only 80,000 units because of an extended plant shutdown. How much fixed overhead should be allocated to each unit produced?
questions.exp: ASC 330-10-30-3 allocates fixed overhead based on normal capacity: $600,000 / 100,000 = $6.00 per unit, and the unallocated $120,000 is expensed. Dividing by actual production ($7.50) improperly inflates inventory during low production.

questions.q: Under the LIFO conformity rule of IRC Section 472, a company that uses LIFO for federal income tax purposes must generally also do which of the following?
choices: Restate prior-year tax returns to LIFO
Use LIFO in its primary financial statements issued to shareholders and creditors
Report on the FIFO basis in its financial statements
Use LIFO for all inventories, including those held by foreign subsidiaries
questions.exp: IRC Section 472 requires a taxpayer using LIFO for tax purposes to use LIFO in reports to shareholders, partners, other owners or creditors, although supplemental non-LIFO disclosures are allowed. Reporting on a FIFO basis in the primary statements would violate the rule.

questions.q: During a period of rising prices, a LIFO company sells more units than it purchases, liquidating old LIFO layers. What is the effect of the liquidation?
choices: Taxable income decreases
There is no effect on income, only on the balance sheet
Cost of goods sold decreases and net income increases
Cost of goods sold increases and net income decreases
questions.exp: Liquidating old, lower-cost layers matches older costs with current revenue, decreasing COGS and increasing income and taxes. The opposite effect would occur only if older layers were more expensive.

questions.q: A LIFO company reported cost of goods sold of $900,000. Its LIFO reserve was $50,000 at the beginning of the year and $70,000 at the end. What would cost of goods sold have been under FIFO?
questions.exp: FIFO COGS = LIFO COGS - increase in the LIFO reserve = $900,000 - $20,000 = $880,000. Adding the increase gives $920,000; an increasing reserve means FIFO inventory rose more, so FIFO COGS is lower.

questions.q: A company changes its inventory method from LIFO to FIFO. How should the change be reported under ASC 250?
choices: Retrospectively, by applying FIFO to all prior periods presented
As a cumulative-effect adjustment in current net income
Prospectively, from the beginning of the current year
As a change in accounting estimate
questions.exp: A change in accounting principle such as LIFO to FIFO is applied retrospectively unless impracticable. Prospective treatment is typical for a change to LIFO, because LIFO layers for prior years usually cannot be reconstructed.

questions.q: During a period of steadily rising prices and stable inventory quantities, how does FIFO compare with LIFO?
choices: FIFO reports higher ending inventory and higher net income
FIFO reports lower ending inventory and lower net income
FIFO and LIFO report the same net income
FIFO reports higher cost of goods sold and lower income taxes
questions.exp: With rising prices, FIFO assigns older, lower costs to COGS and newer, higher costs to ending inventory, producing higher inventory and income. LIFO produces lower income and lower taxes.

questions.q: In Year 1, a FIFO company wrote inventory down from a cost of $50,000 to its NRV of $42,000. In Year 2, the NRV of the same unsold inventory recovered to $48,000. How should the recovery be accounted for under U.S. GAAP in the annual financial statements?
choices: The inventory remains at $42,000; the written-down amount is the new cost basis
Recognize a $6,000 gain and increase inventory to $48,000
Credit other comprehensive income for $6,000
Recognize an $8,000 gain and restore inventory to $50,000
questions.exp: Under ASC 330-10-35-14, a write-down establishes a new cost basis that is not marked up for later recoveries in annual statements. Reversing the write-down is permitted under IFRS, which is the trap.

questions.q: A company uses the net method to record purchases. It bought merchandise for $10,000 with terms 2/10, n/30 and paid after the discount period. At what amount is the merchandise recorded in inventory?
questions.exp: Under the net method, purchases are recorded net of the available discount, $9,800, and the $200 paid because the discount was missed is recorded as purchase discounts lost, a financing-type expense. Recording $10,000 applies the gross method.

questions.q: A consignor shipped goods costing $30,000 to a consignee and paid $1,500 of freight to the consignee. By year-end, the consignee had sold one-third of the goods. What amount should the consignor include in its year-end inventory?
questions.exp: Goods on consignment remain the consignor's inventory, including freight to the consignee as a cost of the goods: two-thirds x $31,500 = $21,000. Excluding the freight gives $20,000.

questions.q: For which inventory cost flow method will ending inventory always be the same under a periodic system and a perpetual system?
choices: FIFO
Dollar-value LIFO
Weighted average
LIFO
questions.exp: FIFO always leaves the most recent purchases in ending inventory regardless of when sales occur, so periodic and perpetual results match. LIFO and average methods depend on the timing of sales, so periodic and perpetual results can differ.

questions.q: A periodic-system company began the year with 400 units at $5, purchased 600 units at $6 and then 1,000 units at $6.40. It sold 1,500 units. What is cost of goods sold under the weighted-average method?
questions.exp: Weighted-average cost = $12,000 / 2,000 units = $6.00; COGS = 1,500 x $6.00 = $9,000. FIFO gives $8,800, LIFO gives $9,400, and $8,700 uses a simple (unweighted) average of the unit prices.

questions.q: A company had cost of goods sold of $600,000, beginning inventory of $100,000 and ending inventory of $140,000. Using a 365-day year, what is the average number of days' sales in inventory?
choices: 85 days
5 days
73 days
61 days
questions.exp: Inventory turnover = $600,000 / [($100,000 + $140,000) / 2] = 5 times; days in inventory = 365 / 5 = 73 days. Using ending inventory alone gives about 85 days.

questions.q: At year-end, a company received goods purchased on credit for $25,000 but neither recorded the purchase nor included the goods in its physical count. What is the effect on the current year's financial statements?
choices: Net income understated by $25,000
No effect on any amounts
Net income overstated by $25,000
No effect on net income; inventory and accounts payable both understated by $25,000
questions.exp: Purchases and ending inventory are both understated by $25,000, so COGS and net income are unaffected, but inventory and accounts payable are each understated. Looking only at the missing inventory leads to the income-understated trap.

questions.q: Under ASC 330, for which inventory methods is inventory measured at the lower of cost or market (using replacement cost with a ceiling and a floor) rather than the lower of cost and net realizable value?
choices: LIFO and the retail inventory method
All inventory methods
FIFO and weighted average
Specific identification only
questions.exp: ASU 2015-11 simplified measurement to lower of cost and NRV for all methods except LIFO and the retail inventory method, which still use lower of cost or market. Assuming the old model still applies to all methods is the trap.

questions.q: Which inventory cost flow assumption is prohibited under IFRS but permitted under U.S. GAAP?
choices: FIFO
LIFO
Specific identification
Weighted average
questions.exp: IAS 2 prohibits LIFO, while U.S. GAAP permits it. FIFO, weighted average and, for items not ordinarily interchangeable, specific identification are permitted under both frameworks.

questions.q: A LIFO company applies lower of cost or market to an item with a cost of $60, replacement cost of $58, selling price of $65, costs to sell of $10 and a normal profit margin of $8. At what amount should the item be reported?
questions.exp: The ceiling is NRV of $65 - $10 = $55 and the floor is $55 - $8 = $47; replacement cost of $58 exceeds the ceiling, so market is $55, which is below the $60 cost. Using unadjusted replacement cost of $58 ignores the ceiling.

questions.q: In its second-quarter interim financial statements, a LIFO company liquidated part of a base-period layer, but it expects to replace the liquidated units before the end of the fiscal year. How should cost of goods sold for the quarter be determined?
choices: Using the expected replacement cost of the liquidated units
Using the average cost of all purchases during the quarter
Using the historical cost of the liquidated LIFO layer
Using FIFO cost for the liquidated units
questions.exp: ASC 270-10-45-6 requires that a temporary interim liquidation of a LIFO base-period layer expected to be replaced by year-end be charged to COGS at expected replacement cost, not the old layer cost. Using the historical layer cost would overstate interim income for a liquidation that will reverse.

questions.q: On January 1, Year 1, a company purchased $100,000 face value, five-year, 8% bonds (interest paid annually on December 31) for $92,418, a price that yields 10%. It classifies the bonds as held to maturity. What is the carrying amount of the investment at December 31, Year 1?
questions.exp: Interest income = $92,418 x 10% = $9,242; cash received = $8,000; discount amortization = $1,242; carrying amount = $93,660 (ASC 310-20 effective interest method). Straight-line amortization ($7,582 / 5 = $1,516) gives $93,934.

questions.q: On January 1, a company purchased $100,000 face value, five-year, 7% bonds for $105,000, yielding 6%, and classified them as held to maturity. Interest is paid annually. What is the carrying amount of the bonds after the first interest payment?
questions.exp: Interest income = $105,000 x 6% = $6,300, less cash interest of $7,000, amortizes $700 of premium: $105,000 - $700 = $104,300. Straight-line amortization of the $5,000 premium over five years gives $104,000.

questions.q: In Year 1, a company purchased available-for-sale debt securities for $200,000; their fair value at December 31, Year 1 was $215,000. In Year 2, it sold them for $212,000. Ignoring taxes and amortization, what gain should be recognized in net income in Year 2?
choices: $3,000 loss
questions.exp: The realized gain on sale of an AFS security is proceeds less amortized cost: $212,000 - $200,000 = $12,000, and the $15,000 previously in AOCI is reclassified out. Measuring against the prior fair value of $215,000 gives the $3,000 loss trap, which applies to trading securities.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a reclassification adjustment in reporting other comprehensive income for available-for-sale debt securities?
choices: To adjust for income taxes on unrealized gains
To avoid double counting gains or losses that were in OCI in an earlier period and are realized in net income in the current period
To reclassify AFS securities to the trading category
To transfer unrealized gains to retained earnings at year-end
questions.exp: When an AFS security is sold, the previously recognized unrealized gain or loss is removed from OCI so it is not counted in comprehensive income twice (ASC 220-10-45-15). It is not a tax adjustment or a transfer to retained earnings.

questions.q: A company holds trading debt securities with a cost of $150,000. Their fair value was $160,000 at December 31, Year 1 and $155,000 at December 31, Year 2. There were no purchases or sales in Year 2. What amount is reported in Year 2 net income related to the change in fair value?
choices: $5,000 unrealized gain
$5,000 unrealized loss in other comprehensive income
$0, because fair value still exceeds cost
$5,000 unrealized loss
questions.exp: Trading securities are remeasured to fair value each period with changes in net income: $155,000 - $160,000 = $5,000 loss. Comparing fair value with original cost ignores the Year 1 adjustment already recognized.

questions.q: A company purchased 1,000 shares of another company's common stock (less than 1% ownership) for $50 per share. During the year, it received dividends of $2 per share, and the stock's fair value at year-end was $56 per share. What total amount is recognized in net income for the year?
questions.exp: Under ASC 321, equity securities with readily determinable fair values are measured at fair value through net income, so the $6,000 increase plus $2,000 of dividend income is $8,000. Reporting the $6,000 in OCI applies the AFS model eliminated for equity securities by ASU 2016-01.

questions.q: A company owns equity securities without a readily determinable fair value and elected the measurement alternative; they were recorded at a cost of $300,000. During the year, an orderly transaction in a similar security of the same issuer indicated a value of $340,000. What should the company record?
choices: A $40,000 gain in net income, increasing the carrying amount to $340,000
Disclosure of the $340,000 value only
A $40,000 unrealized gain in other comprehensive income
No adjustment; the securities remain at cost
questions.exp: Under the measurement alternative in ASC 321-10-35-2, the investment is cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for identical or similar investments of the same issuer, with changes in net income. OCI is not used for equity securities.

questions.q: Under the measurement alternative for an equity security without a readily determinable fair value, qualitative indicators suggest impairment. The investment's carrying amount is $250,000 and its fair value is estimated at $180,000. What should be recognized?
choices: A $70,000 impairment loss in net income
A $70,000 loss in other comprehensive income
Nothing unless the decline is other than temporary
Nothing until the security is sold
questions.exp: ASC 321-10-35-3 requires a single-step qualitative assessment; if impaired, the security is written down to fair value with the loss in net income. The other-than-temporary concept was removed for these securities by ASU 2016-01.

questions.q: Which investment may be classified as held to maturity?
choices: Common stock the company intends to hold indefinitely
A debt security the company has the positive intent and ability to hold to maturity
Preferred stock that is not mandatorily redeemable
A debt security the company may sell if interest rates change
questions.exp: ASC 320-10-25-1 permits HTM classification only for debt securities the entity has the positive intent and ability to hold to maturity. Equity securities have no maturity, and a security that may be sold in response to interest rate changes cannot be HTM.

questions.q: A company transfers a debt security from held to maturity to available for sale when its amortized cost is $500,000 and its fair value is $520,000. How is the $20,000 difference reported at the date of transfer?
choices: As unrealized holding gain in other comprehensive income
It is not recognized until the security is sold
As a gain in net income
As an adjustment to retained earnings
questions.exp: On transfer from HTM to AFS, the unrealized holding gain or loss at the transfer date is recognized in OCI (ASC 320-10-35-10). Recognizing it in net income applies the rule for transfers into the trading category.

questions.q: A company sells a held-to-maturity debt security before maturity in response to a change in its investment strategy. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The sale has no effect on other HTM securities
The sale calls into question the company's intent to hold its other debt securities to maturity, which may require reclassifying them
The gain or loss is deferred until the original maturity date
The security must be restated as trading for all prior periods
questions.exp: Sales of HTM securities for reasons other than those permitted by ASC 320-10-25-6, such as significant credit deterioration, call into question the entity's intent and can taint the HTM portfolio. A change in investment strategy is not a permitted reason.

questions.q: On January 1, an investor paid $600,000 for 30% of an investee's common stock, an amount equal to 30% of the investee's book value; the investor has significant influence. The investee reported net income of $200,000 and paid dividends of $50,000 for the year. What is the investment's carrying amount at December 31?
questions.exp: Under the equity method, $600,000 + 30% x $200,000 - 30% x $50,000 = $645,000 (ASC 323-10-35-4). Treating dividends as income instead of a reduction of the investment gives $660,000.

questions.q: An investor paid $1,000,000 for 25% of an investee with book value of net assets of $3,200,000. The $200,000 excess of cost over book value relates $120,000 to equipment with a 10-year remaining life and $80,000 to goodwill. The investee's net income for the year was $400,000. What equity method income should the investor recognize?
questions.exp: Share of net income is $100,000, less excess depreciation on the equipment of $120,000 / 10 = $12,000, equals $88,000. Equity method goodwill is not amortized, so amortizing it too gives $80,000.

questions.q: An investor paid $900,000 for 30% of an investee whose net assets had a book value of $2,500,000. The entire excess of cost over the investor's share of book value relates to investee land. The investee's net income for the year was $300,000. What equity method income should the investor report?
questions.exp: The $150,000 excess ($900,000 - $750,000) relates to land, which is not depreciated, so equity income is 30% x $300,000 = $90,000. Amortizing the land differential (for example, $150,000 / 10 years) would incorrectly reduce income.

questions.q: An investor owns 40% of an investee. During the year, the investor sold inventory costing $60,000 to the investee for $100,000, and 25% of that inventory remains unsold by the investee at year-end. The investee's net income was $300,000. What equity method income should the investor report?
questions.exp: Unrealized profit in the investee's ending inventory is $40,000 x 25% = $10,000, and the investor eliminates its 40% share, $4,000: $120,000 - $4,000 = $116,000 (ASC 323-10-35-7). Eliminating the full $10,000 confuses the equity method with consolidation.

questions.q: An investor owns 30% of an investee's common stock. The investee reported net income of $500,000 and has cumulative preferred stock outstanding, held by others, with annual dividends of $100,000; no preferred dividends were declared this year. What equity method income should the investor recognize?
