questions.exp: The investor's share is computed after deducting cumulative preferred dividends, whether or not declared: 30% x ($500,000 - $100,000) = $120,000 (ASC 323-10-35-16). Ignoring the undeclared cumulative dividends gives $150,000.

questions.q: On July 1, an investor acquired 30% of an investee and obtained significant influence. The investee reported net income of $400,000 for the calendar year, earned evenly. What equity method income should the investor report for the year?
questions.exp: The investor records only its share of income earned after acquisition: 30% x $400,000 x 6/12 = $60,000. Recording a full year's share ($120,000) includes income earned before the investor owned the shares.

questions.q: An equity method investment has a carrying amount of $50,000. The investor's share of the investee's current-year loss is $80,000. The investor has not guaranteed the investee's obligations and is not committed to provide further support. What loss should the investor recognize?
choices: $80,000, reducing the investment to a $30,000 credit balance
$0, because losses are not recognized under the equity method
$50,000, reducing the investment to zero
questions.exp: Under ASC 323-10-35-19 and 35-20, the investor stops applying the equity method when the investment reaches zero unless it has guaranteed obligations or committed to support; it resumes only after its share of later income exceeds the unrecognized losses. Recognizing a negative investment is the trap.

questions.q: An investor that held 10% of an investee purchased an additional 20%, obtaining significant influence. Under current U.S. GAAP, how should the investor begin applying the equity method?
choices: Record a cumulative-effect adjustment to retained earnings
Retroactively restate prior periods as if the equity method had always applied
Continue to measure the original 10% at fair value and apply the equity method only to the new 20%
Add the cost of the additional interest to the current basis of the previously held interest and apply the equity method prospectively
questions.exp: ASU 2016-07 (ASC 323-10-35-33) eliminated retroactive adjustment; the investor adds the cost of the new interest to its existing basis and applies the equity method prospectively. Retroactive restatement was required before 2017.

questions.q: An investor elects the fair value option for an investment that would otherwise be accounted for under the equity method. How is the investment subsequently measured?
choices: At fair value, with changes in fair value reported in net income
At fair value, with changes reported in other comprehensive income
Using the equity method, with fair value disclosed
At cost less impairment
questions.exp: Under ASC 825-10, an entity electing the fair value option measures the instrument at fair value with unrealized gains and losses in earnings, and the election is irrevocable. OCI treatment applies to AFS debt securities, not fair value option items.

questions.q: An investor owns 25% of an investee's voting stock, but the investee has filed a lawsuit challenging the investor's ability to exercise influence, and the investor has signed an agreement surrendering significant shareholder rights. How should the investor most likely account for the investment?
choices: As an equity security under ASC 321, because the presumption of significant influence is overcome
Consolidation
Equity method, because ownership exceeds 20%
As a held-to-maturity investment
questions.exp: The 20% presumption of significant influence can be overcome by evidence such as investee opposition or a standstill agreement surrendering shareholder rights (ASC 323-10-15-10). Applying the equity method mechanically based on percentage ignores that evidence.

questions.q: An investor owns 15% of an investee's common stock. It holds a seat on the investee's board, participates in policy-making and exchanges managerial personnel with the investee. How should the investment most likely be accounted for?
choices: Using the equity method, because the investor can exercise significant influence
Using consolidation
At fair value through net income, because ownership is below 20%
At amortized cost
questions.exp: Significant influence can exist below 20% when indicated by board representation, participation in policy-making and interchange of managerial personnel (ASC 323-10-15-6). Applying the 20% threshold mechanically is the trap.

questions.q: On April 1, a company purchased $100,000 face value, 6% bonds at 102 plus accrued interest. Interest is paid semiannually on June 30 and December 31. How much cash did the company pay?
questions.exp: The price is $102,000 plus three months of accrued interest ($100,000 x 6% x 3/12 = $1,500), totaling $103,500; the accrued interest is a receivable recovered on June 30. Omitting accrued interest gives $102,000.

questions.q: The fair value of a company's held-to-maturity debt securities declined by $40,000 during the year because market interest rates rose; there are no expected credit losses. How should the decline be reported?
choices: As a $40,000 loss in other comprehensive income
It is not recognized in the financial statements, although fair value is disclosed
As a reduction of the securities' amortized cost through an allowance
As a $40,000 loss in net income
questions.exp: HTM securities are carried at amortized cost, so interest-rate-driven fair value declines are not recognized, though fair value is disclosed (ASC 320-10-35-1). Recognizing the decline in OCI applies the AFS model.

questions.q: An investor applies the equity method to its 30% investment. During the year, the investee reported a $50,000 unrealized gain on available-for-sale debt securities in its other comprehensive income. How should the investor report its share?
choices: It is not recorded until the investee sells the securities
As $50,000 in the investor's other comprehensive income
As $15,000 in the investor's other comprehensive income and an increase in the investment
As $15,000 of equity method income in net income
questions.exp: Under ASC 323-10-35-18, an investor records its proportionate share of the investee's OCI items in its own OCI, increasing the investment: 30% x $50,000 = $15,000. Including it in equity method income mixes OCI with net income.

questions.q: An investor determines that the fair value of its equity method investment has declined below carrying amount and that the decline is other than temporary. In a later period, the investment's fair value recovers. How should the investor account for these events?
choices: Recognize an impairment loss and reverse it upon recovery, up to the original carrying amount
Record the impairment in OCI and reverse it when value recovers
Ignore the decline because equity method investments are not tested for impairment
Recognize an impairment loss in earnings and do not reverse it upon recovery
questions.exp: ASC 323-10-35-32 requires recognizing other-than-temporary declines in value of an equity method investment in earnings, and the write-down is not reversed later. Reversal is the trap, borrowed from IFRS or held-for-sale accounting.

questions.q: A company purchased an available-for-sale debt security with a face value of $100,000 for $104,000. During Year 1, it amortized $800 of premium. At year-end the security's fair value was $101,000, and there is no credit loss. What unrealized holding loss is reported in other comprehensive income for Year 1?
questions.exp: Amortized cost = $104,000 - $800 = $103,200; unrealized loss = $103,200 - $101,000 = $2,200. Comparing fair value with original cost ($3,000) double counts the $800 already recognized in interest income through premium amortization.

questions.q: How is interest income on an available-for-sale debt security purchased at a discount computed?
choices: Using the effective interest method on the security's fair value at the start of the period
As the change in fair value plus the cash coupon received
As the cash coupon received, with no discount amortization
Using the effective interest method on amortized cost, unaffected by fair value adjustments
questions.exp: AFS debt securities recognize interest income under the effective interest method on amortized cost, the same as HTM securities; the fair value adjustment is a separate OCI entry. Basing interest on fair value mixes the two measurements.

questions.q: An investor sold its entire 30% equity method investment, which had a carrying amount of $645,000, for $700,000 cash. There are no related amounts in the investor's accumulated other comprehensive income. What gain should the investor recognize?
choices: $0, with the difference credited to additional paid-in capital
questions.exp: The gain on sale is the proceeds less the carrying amount of the equity method investment: $700,000 - $645,000 = $55,000. Taking 30% of the difference ($16,500) wrongly applies the ownership percentage a second time.

questions.q: A company reported a $40,000 pretax unrealized holding gain on available-for-sale debt securities during the year. Its tax rate is 25%. What amount should be reported in other comprehensive income for the gain?
choices: $0, because the gain is unrealized
questions.exp: OCI items are reported net of the related tax effect (or before tax with the tax shown separately): $40,000 x (1 - 25%) = $30,000 (ASC 220-10-45-12). Reporting $40,000 ignores the deferred tax on the unrealized gain.

questions.q: A lessee signs a five-year finance lease requiring annual payments of $50,000 at the beginning of each year. The lessee's discount rate is 8%; the present value factor for an annuity due of five periods at 8% is 4.3121, and for an ordinary annuity it is 3.9927. The lessee also paid $5,000 of initial direct costs. What is the initial lease liability?
questions.exp: Payments at the beginning of each year form an annuity due: $50,000 x 4.3121 = $215,605. Initial direct costs are added to the right-of-use asset ($220,605), not the liability, and the ordinary annuity factor gives the $199,635 trap.

questions.q: A lessee's finance lease liability was $215,605 at commencement on January 1, Year 1, including the first $50,000 annual payment made that day; subsequent payments are due each January 1. The discount rate is 8%. What interest expense should the lessee recognize for Year 1?
questions.exp: The commencement-date payment reduces the liability to $165,605 before any interest accrues: $165,605 x 8% = $13,248. Computing interest on the full $215,605 ignores the payment made at commencement.

questions.q: A lessee recorded a $220,605 right-of-use asset for a five-year finance lease of equipment with an eight-year useful life. The lease transfers ownership of the equipment to the lessee at the end of the lease term. What annual amortization of the ROU asset should be recognized?
questions.exp: When a lease transfers ownership or contains a purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised, the ROU asset is amortized over the asset's useful life: $220,605 / 8 = $27,576 (ASC 842-20-35-8). Amortizing over the five-year lease term gives $44,121.

questions.q: A lessee leases equipment with a fair value of $500,000 and a 10-year remaining economic life for 6 years. The present value of lease payments is $420,000. Ownership does not transfer, there is no purchase option and the asset is not specialized. Using the 75% and 90% thresholds as reasonable approaches to the classification criteria, how should the lessee classify the lease?
choices: Operating lease, because none of the finance lease criteria is met
Finance lease, because the lease term is a major part of the economic life
Finance lease, because the present value of payments is substantially all of fair value
Short-term lease
questions.exp: The lease term is 60% of the economic life (below 75%) and the payments' present value is 84% of fair value (below 90%), and the other criteria are not met, so it is an operating lease (ASC 842-10-25-2). Short-term leases are those of 12 months or less.

questions.q: A lessee signs a three-year operating lease with annual payments, made at the end of each year, of $30,000, $33,000 and $36,000. What lease cost should the lessee recognize in Year 1?
questions.exp: Operating lease cost is recognized as a single straight-line amount over the term: $99,000 / 3 = $33,000 (ASC 842-20-25-6). Recognizing the $30,000 cash payment ignores straight-line recognition.

questions.q: A retailer signs a five-year operating lease for store space. The lessor grants the first year rent-free, and the retailer pays $60,000 per year for Years 2 through 5. What lease cost should the retailer recognize in Year 1?
questions.exp: Total payments of $240,000 are recognized straight-line over five years, $48,000 per year, including the rent-free year. Recognizing nothing in Year 1 follows cash rather than the straight-line requirement.

questions.q: A lessee recognized an operating lease liability and ROU asset of $87,898 for a three-year lease with end-of-year payments of $30,000, $33,000 and $36,000, using a 6% discount rate. Straight-line lease cost is $33,000 per year. What is the ROU asset at the end of Year 1?
questions.exp: Liability = $87,898 + $5,274 interest accretion - $30,000 = $63,172; ROU amortization is the plug $33,000 - $5,274 = $27,726, leaving $60,172 (equivalently, the liability less $3,000 of accrued rent). The $63,172 trap is the liability balance.

questions.q: A lessee leases office equipment for a noncancelable term of 10 months with no purchase option and has elected the short-term lease exemption for that asset class. How should the lessee account for the lease?
choices: Recognize lease payments as expense on a straight-line basis without recognizing an ROU asset or lease liability
Recognize an ROU asset and lease liability measured at the present value of payments
Recognize an ROU asset but no liability
Recognize a finance lease
questions.exp: ASC 842-20-25-2 allows lessees to elect, by asset class, not to recognize ROU assets and liabilities for leases of 12 months or less without a purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised. Recognizing the asset and liability ignores the elected exemption.

questions.q: A public business entity lessee cannot readily determine the rate implicit in a lease. Which discount rate should it use to measure the lease liability?
choices: Its incremental borrowing rate
The lessor's incremental borrowing rate
The risk-free rate
The prime rate
questions.exp: ASC 842-20-30-3 requires the implicit rate if readily determinable, and otherwise the lessee's incremental borrowing rate. The risk-free rate election is available only to lessees that are not public business entities.

questions.q: A store lease requires fixed payments of $100,000 per year, an annual increase tied to the Consumer Price Index, and additional rent of 2% of the store's annual sales. How are the variable payments treated in initially measuring the lessee's lease liability?
choices: Neither is considered; only the $100,000 is included, with no CPI measurement
Payments are measured using the CPI at commencement, and the sales-based rent is excluded and expensed as incurred
Both the CPI increases and the sales-based rent are estimated and included
The sales-based rent is included and the CPI increases are excluded
questions.exp: Variable payments that depend on an index are included using the index at commencement, while payments based on performance or usage are excluded and recognized when incurred (ASC 842-10-30-5). Estimating future sales-based rent is the trap.

questions.q: A lessee guarantees that the leased equipment will be worth $50,000 at the end of the lease. At commencement, the lessee expects the equipment to be worth $40,000. What amount related to the residual value guarantee is included in the lessee's lease payments?
questions.exp: A lessee includes amounts probable of being owed under a residual value guarantee: $50,000 - $40,000 = $10,000 (ASC 842-10-30-5). Including the full guaranteed amount applies the lessor's perspective.

questions.q: A lease contains a purchase option at a price far below the asset's expected fair value at that date, so the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise it. How does this affect the lessee's accounting?
choices: The lease is automatically classified as an operating lease
The exercise price is excluded from lease payments until exercised
The option is disclosed only
The exercise price is included in lease payments, the lease is a finance lease, and the ROU asset is amortized over the asset's useful life
questions.exp: A purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised is a finance lease criterion, its exercise price is included in lease payments, and amortization is over the useful life (ASC 842-10-25-2 and 842-20-35-8). Excluding the price until exercise understates the liability.

questions.q: A lease has a noncancelable period of five years and a three-year renewal at the lessee's option. Because the lessee has made significant leasehold improvements, it is reasonably certain to renew. A further two-year renewal is not reasonably certain. What is the lease term?
choices: 8 years
10 years
3 years
5 years
questions.exp: The lease term includes the noncancelable period plus renewal periods the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise: 5 + 3 = 8 years (ASC 842-10-30-1). Including the second renewal, which is not reasonably certain, gives 10 years.

questions.q: In connection with signing a lease, a lessee paid a $6,000 commission to a broker, allocated $4,000 of internal salaries for employees who negotiated the lease, and paid $3,000 of legal fees for advice that would have been incurred even if the lease had not been executed. What are the initial direct costs?
questions.exp: ASC 842 defines initial direct costs as incremental costs that would not have been incurred had the lease not been obtained, such as the $6,000 commission. Internal salaries and legal fees incurred regardless are excluded.

questions.q: A lessee's lease liability at commencement is $300,000. Before commencement, it prepaid $20,000 of rent to the lessor. It received a $15,000 lease incentive from the lessor and incurred $5,000 of initial direct costs. What is the initial right-of-use asset?
questions.exp: ROU asset = liability $300,000 + prepaid payments $20,000 - incentives received $15,000 + initial direct costs $5,000 = $310,000 (ASC 842-20-30-5). Adding the incentive rather than subtracting it gives $340,000.

questions.q: A manufacturer leases equipment to a customer in a sales-type lease. The equipment's fair value is $500,000, its carrying amount is $400,000, the present value of lease payments is $500,000 and there is no residual value. What selling profit should the lessor recognize at commencement?
choices: $0, deferred over the lease term
questions.exp: In a sales-type lease, selling profit of $500,000 - $400,000 = $100,000 is recognized at commencement (ASC 842-30-25-1). Deferring profit over the term applies to direct financing leases.

questions.q: In a sales-type lease, the leased asset has a fair value of $500,000 and a carrying amount of $400,000. The present value of lease payments is $460,000 and the present value of the unguaranteed residual is $40,000. What revenue should the lessor recognize at commencement?
questions.exp: Revenue is the lesser of fair value or the present value of lease payments, $460,000; cost of sales is the carrying amount less the present value of the unguaranteed residual, $360,000. Using fair value as revenue includes the residual the lessee has not paid for.

questions.q: A lease is classified by the lessor as a direct financing lease because a third party guaranteed the residual value. The asset's fair value exceeds its carrying amount. How is the selling profit treated?
choices: Deferred and included in the net investment, recognized over the lease term
Recognized immediately at commencement
Recognized when the residual value is realized
Never recognized
questions.exp: ASC 842-30-25-8 requires selling profit on a direct financing lease to be deferred and recognized over the term by reducing the net investment, while a selling loss is recognized immediately. Immediate recognition is the sales-type treatment.

questions.q: A lessor leases a building under an operating lease with escalating rents. How does the lessor account for the lease?
choices: Continues to depreciate the building and recognizes lease income on a straight-line basis
Recognizes the present value of all rents as income at commencement
Records rental income equal to cash received each period and stops depreciating the building
Derecognizes the building and records a net investment in the lease
questions.exp: Under ASC 842-30-25-11, an operating lessor keeps the underlying asset on its books, continues depreciating it and recognizes lease income straight-line over the term. Derecognizing the asset is sales-type or direct financing lease accounting.

questions.q: A company sells a building with a carrying amount of $600,000 to a buyer for its fair value of $800,000 and leases it back for five years under an operating lease. The transfer qualifies as a sale under ASC 606, and there is no repurchase option. What gain should the seller-lessee recognize?
choices: $40,000 per year over five years
$200,000 deferred and amortized in proportion to the ROU asset
$0, deferred over the leaseback term
$200,000 at the date of sale
questions.exp: When a sale-leaseback qualifies as a sale at fair value, ASC 842-40-25-4 requires the seller-lessee to recognize the full gain immediately. Deferring the gain over the leaseback term was the ASC 840 approach.

questions.q: A company sells equipment and leases it back. The agreement gives the seller-lessee an option to repurchase the equipment at a fixed price, and the equipment is not readily available in the marketplace. How should the seller-lessee account for the transaction?
choices: As a failed sale: keep the equipment on its books and record the cash received as a financial liability
As a sale, with any gain recognized immediately
As a lease with no recognition of the cash received
As a sale, with the gain deferred until the repurchase right expires
questions.exp: A repurchase option precludes sale accounting unless the exercise price is fair value at exercise and the asset is not specialized and is readily available (ASC 842-40-25-3), so the transaction is a financing. Recognizing a sale ignores that control has not transferred.

questions.q: A company sells a building with a carrying amount of $600,000 and a fair value of $800,000 for $750,000 and leases it back under an operating lease. The transaction qualifies as a sale. What gain should the seller-lessee recognize?
questions.exp: When the sale price is below fair value, the $50,000 shortfall is treated as a prepayment of rent (added to the ROU asset), and the gain is measured using fair value: $800,000 - $600,000 = $200,000 (ASC 842-40-30-2). Measuring the gain on the stated price gives $150,000.

questions.q: How does a lessee present the expense from a finance lease compared with an operating lease in its income statement?
choices: Finance lease: interest on the liability and amortization of the ROU asset reported separately; operating lease: a single lease cost, generally straight-line
Both report a single straight-line lease cost
Both report interest expense and amortization expense separately
Finance lease: a single lease cost; operating lease: interest and amortization separately
questions.exp: ASC 842-20-45-4 requires finance lease interest and ROU amortization to be presented separately (front-loading total expense), while operating leases produce a single straight-line lease cost within operating expenses. Reversing the two models is the trap.

questions.q: A lessee's contract requires annual payments of $120,000 for equipment and maintenance services. The standalone price of the equipment lease is $110,000 and of the maintenance is $20,000. The lessee has not elected the practical expedient to combine lease and nonlease components. What annual amount is allocated to the lease component?
questions.exp: Consideration is allocated on a relative standalone price basis: $120,000 x $110,000 / $130,000 = $101,538 (ASC 842-10-15-33). Allocating the full $120,000 applies the practical expedient, which was not elected.

questions.q: How must a lessee present right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for finance leases and operating leases on its balance sheet or in the notes?
choices: Only finance leases are recognized; operating leases are disclosed in the notes
They are combined with property, plant and equipment and long-term debt without disclosure
Operating lease liabilities are reported in equity
Finance and operating lease ROU assets and liabilities are presented separately from each other and from other assets and liabilities, or disclosed with their line items
questions.exp: ASC 842-20-45-1 requires finance and operating lease ROU assets and liabilities to be presented separately from each other and from other items, or disclosed with the line items that include them. Off-balance-sheet operating leases ended with ASC 842.

questions.q: A company contracts for the use of rail cars for three years. The supplier may substitute other rail cars at any time, has many alternative cars readily available, and would benefit economically from substituting them. Does the contract contain a lease?
choices: No, because the supplier has a substantive substitution right, so there is no identified asset
Yes, a finance lease, because the term exceeds 12 months
No, because rail cars are not property, plant and equipment
Yes, because the company uses rail cars for three years
questions.exp: A contract contains a lease only if there is an identified asset; a supplier's substantive right to substitute, with practical ability and economic benefit, means no identified asset exists (ASC 842-10-15-10). The length of use alone does not create a lease.

questions.q: A lessee leases 10,000 square feet of office space. Midway through the term, the parties modify the lease to add 5,000 square feet of additional space at a price that reflects its standalone price. How should the lessee account for the modification?
choices: Account for it as a correction of an error
Remeasure the existing lease liability for the combined space
Reclassify the original lease as a finance lease
Account for the additional space as a separate contract
questions.exp: A modification that grants an additional right of use priced at its standalone price is accounted for as a separate contract (ASC 842-10-25-8). Remeasuring the existing lease applies only when the modification is not a separate contract.

questions.q: At commencement of a sales-type lease, a lessor's net investment is $500,000, and the lessee makes the first annual payment of $70,000 that day. The rate implicit in the lease is 8%. What interest income should the lessor recognize for the first year?
questions.exp: Interest income is earned on the net investment after the commencement-date payment: ($500,000 - $70,000) x 8% = $34,400. Computing interest on the full $500,000 ignores the payment received at commencement.

questions.q: A lessee leases equipment that was custom-built to its specifications and is expected to have no alternative use to the lessor at the end of the lease term. The other finance lease criteria are not met. How should the lessee classify the lease?
choices: Short-term lease
Finance lease
Operating lease, because ownership does not transfer
Not a lease, because the asset is specialized
questions.exp: An underlying asset so specialized that it has no alternative use to the lessor at the end of the term is one of the five finance lease criteria in ASC 842-10-25-2, so meeting it alone is sufficient. Concluding that it is an operating lease because ownership does not transfer ignores that only one criterion needs to be met.

questions.q: A lessor enters into a lease that would otherwise be classified as a sales-type lease, but collectibility of the lease payments is not probable at commencement. How does the lessor account for the lease at commencement?
choices: Classify it as a direct financing lease
Recognize the net investment but defer the selling profit
Recognize selling profit and the net investment as usual
Not derecognize the underlying asset, and record lease payments received as a deposit liability until collectibility becomes probable or other conditions are met
questions.exp: ASC 842-30-25-3 requires a lessor to keep the underlying asset on its books and record payments as a deposit liability when collectibility is not probable at commencement, until the criteria are met. Recognizing profit as usual ignores the collectibility requirement.

questions.q: Under ASC 958 as amended by ASU 2016-14, how must a not-for-profit organization classify its net assets on the statement of financial position?
choices: Unrestricted, temporarily restricted, and permanently restricted
Board-designated and undesignated net assets
Operating and nonoperating net assets
Net assets with donor restrictions and net assets without donor restrictions
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 replaced the three classes with two: with donor restrictions and without donor restrictions. Board designations are disclosed within net assets without donor restrictions, since boards cannot impose donor restrictions.

questions.q: In December, Year 1, a donor made an unconditional written pledge of $50,000 to Hope Shelter, payable in March, Year 2, with no stated purpose restriction. How should Hope report the pledge in Year 1?
choices: Contribution revenue without donor restrictions
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions
No revenue until the cash is received
Deferred revenue (a liability)
questions.exp: An unconditional promise to give is recognized as revenue when received. A pledge payable in a future period carries an implied time restriction, so it is reported as with donor restrictions until received (ASC 958-605-45-5). Waiting for the cash applies the rule for conditional promises.

questions.q: A foundation promised River Museum $200,000, but only if the museum raises $200,000 from other donors by December 31; if the museum fails, the foundation will give nothing. By December 31, the museum had raised $120,000 from others. How much of the foundation's promise should the museum recognize as revenue for the year?
questions.exp: The promise contains a barrier (the matching requirement) and a release from obligation, so it is conditional and recognized only when the barrier is overcome (ASU 2018-08). Because the match is all-or-nothing and was not met, no revenue is recognized; $120,000 would apply only if the match were dollar-for-dollar.

questions.q: During the year, a CPA volunteered tax services to Bright Futures, an NFP, that it would otherwise have purchased for $10,000. Volunteers also staffed a fundraising phone bank; their services were worth $15,000 at minimum wage. What amount of contributed services should Bright Futures recognize?
questions.exp: Contributed services are recognized only if they create or enhance nonfinancial assets, or require specialized skills, are provided by people with those skills, and would typically be purchased if not donated (ASC 958-605-25-16). The CPA's services qualify; the phone bank volunteers' do not.

questions.q: In Year 1, Care Clinic received a $50,000 cash gift restricted by the donor to its immunization program. During Year 1, the clinic spent $30,000 on immunizations. How should the expense and restriction be reported?
choices: Expense of $50,000 in net assets without donor restrictions
Expense of $30,000 in net assets without donor restrictions, and $30,000 of net assets released from restrictions
No expense until the full $50,000 is spent
Expense of $30,000 in net assets with donor restrictions
questions.exp: All expenses are reported in net assets without donor restrictions. Fulfilling the purpose restriction releases $30,000, reported as a reclassification from with to without donor restrictions (ASC 958-205-45). Expenses are never reported in the with-donor-restrictions class.

questions.q: Under ASU 2016-14, which not-for-profit organizations must present an analysis of expenses by both function and nature?
choices: Only NFPs with revenue above $1 million
Only NFPs that receive federal grants
Only voluntary health and welfare organizations
All not-for-profit organizations
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 extended the requirement to all NFPs; the analysis may be presented on the face of the statement of activities, as a separate statement, or in the notes. Before the amendment only voluntary health and welfare organizations had to present a statement of functional expenses.

questions.q: How should a not-for-profit organization report its investment return on the statement of activities?
choices: Gross investment income, with all investment expenses reported as management and general expense
Net of all expenses, including fundraising costs
Net of external and direct internal investment expenses
Only realized gains, with unrealized gains in a separate statement
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 requires investment return to be presented net of external and direct internal investment expenses, and no longer requires disclosure of the netted expenses. Fundraising costs are never netted against investment return.

questions.q: A university's donor-restricted endowment fund has a fair value below the original gift amount (it is underwater). Where should the deficiency be reported under ASU 2016-14?
choices: In net assets without donor restrictions
In net assets with donor restrictions
As a reduction of board-designated endowment
As a liability to the donor
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 requires underwater amounts of donor-restricted endowments to be reported within net assets with donor restrictions, with expanded disclosures. Before the amendment, deficiencies were charged to unrestricted net assets.

questions.q: Art League, an NFP, charges members $100 per year in dues. Members receive benefits (magazine, admission, discounts) with a fair value of about $100. How should Art League account for the dues under ASU 2018-08?
choices: As contribution revenue when received
As a liability until the member terminates membership
As exchange revenue recognized over the membership period
As contribution revenue with donor restrictions
questions.exp: When the resource provider receives commensurate value in return, the transaction is an exchange, not a contribution, and revenue is recognized under ASC 606 as the benefits are provided. Dues are a contribution only to the extent they exceed the value of benefits received.

questions.q: Hope Hospital Foundation held a gala, selling 400 tickets at $250 each. The fair value of the dinner and entertainment provided to each attendee was $100. How should the foundation report the ticket revenue?
choices: Contribution revenue of $40,000 and exchange revenue of $60,000
Contribution revenue of $100,000
Contribution revenue of $60,000 and special event (exchange) revenue of $40,000
Special event revenue of $100,000
questions.exp: Each $250 ticket includes a $100 exchange (the dinner) and a $150 contribution: 400 x $150 = $60,000 contribution and 400 x $100 = $40,000 exchange revenue. Reversing the amounts allocates the contribution to the value of benefits received.

questions.q: City Charity received $100,000 from a donor with instructions to transfer it to a specified food bank. City Charity has no variance power and cannot redirect the funds. How should City Charity account for the receipt?
choices: An asset and a liability to the food bank
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions
Disclosure only
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions
questions.exp: A recipient acting as an agent or intermediary without variance power reports the assets and a liability to the specified beneficiary, not contribution revenue (ASC 958-605-25-24). Revenue would be recognized only if City Charity had variance power.

questions.q: United Fund received $500,000 from a donor who designated a specific agency as the beneficiary but explicitly granted United Fund unilateral power to redirect the gift to another beneficiary. How should United Fund account for the receipt?
choices: As an agency transaction with no effect on the statement of activities
As a liability to the designated agency
As deferred revenue until the funds are distributed
As contribution revenue
questions.exp: When the donor explicitly grants variance power, the recipient organization recognizes the asset and contribution revenue (ASC 958-605-25-25). Liability treatment applies when the recipient lacks variance power.

questions.q: Under ASC 958-360 as amended by ASU 2019-03, a museum need not capitalize contributed works of art in its collection if certain conditions are met. Which of the following is one of those conditions?
choices: The items were acquired by purchase rather than donation
Proceeds from sales of collection items are used to acquire other collection items or for direct care of existing collections, per organizational policy
The museum discloses the items' fair value in the notes
The items have a fair value below $5,000
questions.exp: Collection items need not be capitalized if they are held for public exhibition, education, or research for public service, are protected and preserved, and are subject to a policy requiring sale proceeds to be used for acquisitions or direct care (ASU 2019-03 added direct care). There is no dollar threshold.

questions.q: Which of the following is true regarding depreciation of long-lived assets by not-for-profit organizations?
choices: Only NFPs that charge fees for services must record depreciation
NFPs may elect not to record depreciation
NFPs must recognize depreciation on long-lived tangible assets, but not on individual works of art or historical treasures with extraordinarily long lives
Depreciation is recognized only for donated assets
questions.exp: ASC 958-360-35 requires NFPs to depreciate long-lived assets, with an exception for individual works of art or historical treasures whose economic benefit is used up slowly. There is no general option to omit depreciation.

questions.q: Green Trust, an NFP, received a $2,000,000 cash contribution restricted by the donor to constructing a new building. How should the receipt be classified in the statement of cash flows?
choices: Investing activities
Operating activities
Noncash investing and financing activities
Financing activities
questions.exp: Cash contributions restricted by donors for long-term purposes, such as acquiring buildings or establishing endowments, are financing inflows (ASC 230-10-45-14). Unrestricted contributions are operating, and the later construction payments are investing.

questions.q: Hope Shelter paid $40,000 for a direct-mail fundraising campaign in December. The campaign is expected to generate contributions throughout the following year. How should the cost be reported?
choices: As a reduction of contribution revenue
As fundraising expense when incurred
As a program service expense
As a prepaid asset amortized as contributions are received
questions.exp: Fundraising costs are expensed as incurred, even if they are expected to produce contributions in future periods (ASC 958-720-25-4). Netting them against contribution revenue is not permitted.

questions.q: A not-for-profit mails a brochure that includes both an educational message and a request for donations. Which criteria must all be met for part of the joint costs to be allocated to program activities rather than fundraising?
choices: Donor intent, board approval, and content
Purpose, audience, and content
Timing, frequency, and audience
Cost, benefit, and materiality
questions.exp: Under ASC 958-720-45, joint costs may be allocated to program or management functions only if the purpose, audience, and content criteria are all met; otherwise all joint costs are fundraising. Board approval is not a criterion.

questions.q: A donor contributed a building with a fair value of $1,500,000 to Youth Center, an NFP, with no stipulations about its use or how long it must be used. Youth Center has no policy implying time restrictions. How should the contribution be reported?
choices: Contribution revenue without donor restrictions of $1,500,000
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions, released over the building's useful life
No revenue; the building is recorded directly in net assets
As a capital contribution in a separate statement
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 eliminated the option to imply a time restriction on donated long-lived assets; absent donor stipulations, the contribution is reported without donor restrictions. Releasing it over the useful life was the old implied-time-restriction policy.

questions.q: In Year 1, Wellness Center received $80,000 restricted by the donor for the purchase of medical equipment. In Year 2, it bought the equipment and placed it in service; the donor made no other stipulations. When are the net assets released from restriction?
choices: When the equipment is acquired and placed in service in Year 2
When the cash is received in Year 1
Never; the equipment remains in net assets with donor restrictions
Over the equipment's useful life as it is depreciated
questions.exp: Under the placed-in-service approach required by ASU 2016-14, a restriction to acquire long-lived assets expires when the asset is placed in service, absent explicit donor stipulations. Releasing over the useful life required an implied time restriction policy that is no longer allowed.

questions.q: Under ASU 2016-14, what information about liquidity must a not-for-profit organization disclose?
choices: A projected budget for the next three years
A statement of cash flows using the direct method
Only the amount of cash at year-end
Qualitative information on how it manages liquid resources and quantitative information on the availability of financial assets to meet general expenditures within one year
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 requires qualitative and quantitative liquidity disclosures about financial assets available for general expenditures within one year of the balance sheet date. The direct method is encouraged but not required.

questions.q: On December 31, Year 1, Shelter Inc. received unconditional pledges of $500,000 collectible in 3 years. It estimates 10% will be uncollectible. The present value factor at an appropriate 5% rate for 3 years is 0.8638. What contribution revenue should Shelter recognize in Year 1?
questions.exp: Pledges are measured at the present value of the estimated cash flows to be collected: $500,000 x 90% x 0.8638 = $388,710 (ASC 958-310). $431,900 discounts the pledges but ignores the expected uncollectible amounts.

questions.q: How should a not-for-profit organization measure its investments in equity securities with readily determinable fair values?
choices: At fair value, with gains and losses reported in the statement of activities
At the lower of cost or market
At cost, with impairment losses recognized
Using the equity method, regardless of ownership percentage
questions.exp: ASC 958-320 requires such equity securities and all debt securities to be measured at fair value, with gains and losses reported in the statement of activities as changes in net assets. Unlike business entities, NFPs have no available-for-sale OCI category.

questions.q: A pharmaceutical company donated medical supplies with a fair value of $25,000 to Health Clinic, an NFP, which used all of them in its patient care program during the year. How should the clinic report the donation?
choices: Contribution revenue of $25,000 and program expense of $25,000
Contribution revenue of $25,000 only
A reduction of program expenses of $25,000
Disclosure only
questions.exp: Contributed nonfinancial assets are recognized as contribution revenue at fair value, and expense is recognized when the supplies are used in the program; ASU 2020-07 also requires them to be presented as a separate line item. Disclosure alone omits a recognizable contribution.

questions.q: Under the functional classification of expenses for a not-for-profit organization, how should the salaries of the accounting and payroll staff be classified?
choices: Membership development
Fundraising (a supporting service)
Management and general (a supporting service)
Program services
questions.exp: Supporting services include management and general, fundraising, and membership development; general administration such as accounting and payroll is management and general. These activities do not directly carry out the organization's mission programs.

questions.q: Trinity Church is the irrevocable beneficiary of a perpetual trust held and controlled by a bank. Trinity will receive the trust's income forever but can never receive the principal. How should Trinity account for its beneficial interest when the trust is established?
choices: No recognition, because a third party controls the trust
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions equal to expected first-year income
An asset and contribution revenue with donor restrictions (perpetual in nature), measured at the fair value of the beneficial interest
Disclosure only
questions.exp: Under ASC 958-605, a beneficiary of a perpetual trust held by a third party recognizes its beneficial interest at fair value as contribution revenue with donor restrictions of a perpetual nature. Distributions received later are reported as investment income.

questions.q: For the year, Elm Society had contributions without donor restrictions of $800,000, contributions with donor restrictions of $300,000, net assets released from restrictions of $200,000, and total expenses of $900,000. What is the change in net assets without donor restrictions?
questions.exp: Without donor restrictions: $800,000 + $200,000 released - $900,000 expenses = $100,000. $200,000 is the change in total net assets ($1,100,000 - $900,000), which wrongly includes the restricted contributions.

questions.q: Under ASU 2018-08, what distinguishes a donor-imposed condition from a donor-imposed restriction?
choices: A condition includes a barrier to be overcome and a right of return or release from obligation; a restriction limits the use of the assets but does not prevent recognition
Conditions apply only to cash gifts; restrictions apply only to noncash gifts
A condition limits how the assets may be used; a restriction creates a barrier to receiving them
There is no difference; both delay revenue recognition
questions.exp: A conditional contribution has both a measurable barrier and a right of return of assets or release from the promisor's obligation; revenue is deferred until the condition is met. A restriction only limits use, so revenue is recognized immediately in net assets with donor restrictions.

questions.q: State law and the donor's terms require that a university's endowment investment gains remain in the endowment until appropriated for expenditure by the board. How should the university classify the current year's investment gains on the donor-restricted endowment?
choices: In other comprehensive income
With donor restrictions until appropriated for expenditure
Without donor restrictions, because the gains are not part of the original gift
As a liability until appropriated
questions.exp: Under ASC 958-205 (UPMIFA guidance), earnings on donor-restricted endowments are classified with donor restrictions until appropriated for expenditure and any purpose restrictions are met. NFPs do not report other comprehensive income.

questions.q: During the year, a local business let Aid Network, an NFP, use office space rent-free; the fair rental value was $24,000. How should Aid Network report the donated use of the space?
choices: Rent expense of $24,000 only
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions of $24,000, never released
Contribution revenue of $24,000 and rent expense of $24,000
Disclosure only
questions.exp: The contributed use of facilities is a contribution of a nonfinancial asset measured at fair rental value, and the space is used as received, so revenue and an equal rent (occupancy) expense are recognized. Expense without revenue would leave the contribution unrecorded.

questions.q: A longtime supporter informed Arts Council that she has named the council as a beneficiary of $1,000,000 in her will. The supporter is alive and the will can be changed at any time. How should Arts Council account for this information?
choices: Contribution revenue with donor restrictions of $1,000,000
No recognition, because an intention to give that can be revoked is not an unconditional promise
A receivable disclosed in the notes at $1,000,000
Contribution revenue of $1,000,000 at present value
questions.exp: A revocable bequest is an intention to give, not an unconditional promise, so it is not recognized until the donor dies and the estate is probated (ASC 958-605-25-8). Recognizing it at present value treats it as a pledge.

questions.q: Alton Co.'s defined benefit pension plan had the following for the year: service cost $200,000; PBO at January 1 $2,000,000; discount rate 5%; fair value of plan assets at January 1 $1,800,000; expected return on plan assets 7%; actual return $90,000; amortization of prior service cost $20,000. There was no net gain or loss in AOCI at January 1. What is net periodic pension cost?
questions.exp: Service cost $200,000 + interest $100,000 ($2,000,000 x 5%) - expected return $126,000 ($1,800,000 x 7%) + prior service cost amortization $20,000 = $194,000 (ASC 715-30). $230,000 wrongly uses the $90,000 actual return; the difference from expected return is deferred in OCI.

questions.q: Under ASC 715 as amended by ASU 2017-07, how should an employer present the components of net periodic pension cost in its income statement?
choices: Service cost with other employee compensation costs; the other components separately, outside income from operations
Service cost in other comprehensive income; the other components in operating expenses
All components outside income from operations
All components together within operating expenses
questions.exp: ASU 2017-07 requires service cost to be reported with other compensation costs for the employees' services, and the other components (interest, expected return, amortization) to be presented separately outside any subtotal of income from operations. Reporting all components together in operating expense was the old practice.

questions.q: At December 31, Birk Co.'s pension plan had a projected benefit obligation of $5,000,000, an accumulated benefit obligation of $4,500,000, and plan assets with a fair value of $4,200,000. What net pension liability should Birk report?
questions.exp: The funded status reported on the balance sheet is PBO less the fair value of plan assets: $5,000,000 - $4,200,000 = $800,000 (ASC 715-30). $300,000 incorrectly uses the ABO, which is not the measure for the balance sheet.

questions.q: At January 1, Cass Co. had an unrecognized net loss of $600,000 in AOCI, a PBO of $4,000,000, and a market-related value of plan assets of $3,500,000. The average remaining service period of active employees is 10 years. What is the minimum amortization of the net loss for the year?
questions.exp: The corridor is 10% of the greater of beginning PBO or market-related value: $400,000. The excess $200,000 / 10 years = $20,000. $25,000 bases the corridor on plan assets, the smaller amount, and $60,000 ignores the corridor.

questions.q: Dane Co.'s PBO was $3,000,000 at January 1. During the year, service cost was $250,000, interest cost was $150,000, benefits paid were $200,000, and an actuarial loss from a change in assumptions was $80,000. What is the PBO at December 31?
questions.exp: $3,000,000 + $250,000 + $150,000 + $80,000 - $200,000 = $3,280,000. $3,120,000 treats the actuarial loss as a gain; a loss increases the obligation.

questions.q: Eton Co.'s plan assets had a fair value of $2,500,000 at January 1. During the year, the expected return was $175,000, the actual return was $200,000, employer contributions were $300,000, and benefits paid were $180,000. What is the fair value of plan assets at December 31?
questions.exp: Plan assets increase by the actual return and contributions and decrease by benefits paid: $2,500,000 + $200,000 + $300,000 - $180,000 = $2,820,000. $2,795,000 uses the expected return, which applies only in computing pension cost.

questions.q: On January 1, Fore Co. amended its defined benefit plan to grant credit for prior employee service, increasing the PBO by $600,000. How should Fore initially account for the prior service cost?
choices: Expense the full $600,000 in the year of the amendment
Recognize it in other comprehensive income and amortize it into pension cost over the future service of affected employees
Charge $600,000 directly to retained earnings
Defer it as an intangible asset amortized over 15 years
questions.exp: Prior service cost is recognized in OCI when the amendment occurs (increasing the pension liability) and amortized into net periodic cost over the remaining service period of employees expected to benefit (ASC 715-30). Immediate expensing is not permitted.

questions.q: For the year, Gale Co.'s pension plan assets had an expected return of $126,000 and an actual return of $90,000. There were no other gains or losses. How should Gale account for the difference?
choices: Ignore the difference until plan assets are sold
Increase pension expense by $36,000
Recognize a $36,000 net loss in other comprehensive income
Recognize a $36,000 net gain in other comprehensive income
questions.exp: Pension cost includes the expected return; an actual return below expected ($36,000 shortfall) is an asset loss recognized in OCI and subject to later corridor amortization. Adding it to pension expense immediately defeats the smoothing in ASC 715.

questions.q: Hyde Co. sponsors a defined contribution plan that requires it to contribute 5% of covered salaries. Covered salaries for the year were $2,000,000, and Hyde paid $80,000 to the plan during the year. What pension expense and liability should Hyde report?
choices: Expense $80,000; liability $20,000
Expense $100,000; liability $20,000
Expense $80,000; liability $0
Expense $100,000; liability $0
questions.exp: For a defined contribution plan, expense equals the required contribution for the period, $2,000,000 x 5% = $100,000; the $20,000 unpaid is a liability (ASC 715-70). Expensing only the cash paid uses the cash basis.

questions.q: What distinguishes the projected benefit obligation (PBO) from the accumulated benefit obligation (ABO)?
choices: The PBO excludes service rendered to date
The PBO is undiscounted, while the ABO is discounted
The PBO is measured using future compensation levels, while the ABO uses current compensation levels
The PBO includes only vested benefits
questions.exp: Both are discounted measures of benefits earned for service to date, but the PBO reflects projected future salary increases while the ABO uses current salaries. The vested benefit obligation, not the PBO, is limited to vested benefits.

questions.q: Under ASC 715, what discount rate should be used to measure the projected benefit obligation?
choices: The employer's incremental borrowing rate
The risk-free rate on 30-year Treasury securities
The expected long-term rate of return on plan assets
Rates at which the pension benefits could be effectively settled, such as yields on high-quality fixed-income investments
questions.exp: The discount rate reflects rates at which benefits could be effectively settled, commonly the yields on high-quality corporate bonds matching the benefit payments (ASC 715-30). The expected return on assets is used only for the expected return component.

questions.q: Under a postretirement health care plan, an employee becomes fully eligible for benefits at age 60. The employee was hired at age 30, is now 40, and the expected postretirement benefit obligation (EPBO) for the employee is $120,000. Benefits are attributed evenly over the attribution period. What is the accumulated postretirement benefit obligation (APBO) for this employee?
questions.exp: The attribution period runs from the date of hire to the full eligibility date (30 years); with 10 years served, APBO = $120,000 x 10/30 = $40,000 (ASC 715-60). The EPBO of $120,000 includes service not yet rendered.

questions.q: Ives Co. participates in a multiemployer defined benefit plan for its union employees. How should Ives generally account for its participation?
choices: Disclose the plan without recognizing any expense
Recognize its share of the plan's underfunded status on the balance sheet
Apply single-employer accounting for its proportionate share of plan assets and obligations
Recognize the required contribution for the period as pension cost and any unpaid contributions as a liability
questions.exp: Under ASC 715-80, a participant in a multiemployer plan recognizes its required contribution for the period as net pension cost and a liability for any contributions due and unpaid. It does not record a share of the plan's funded status unless withdrawal is probable.

questions.q: During the year, the discount rate used to measure Jory Co.'s pension obligation increased from 4.5% to 5.5%. All else equal, what is the effect?
choices: The PBO decreases, and an actuarial gain is recognized in OCI
The PBO increases, and service cost is adjusted
The PBO increases, and an actuarial loss is recognized in OCI
The PBO decreases, and a gain is recognized immediately in net income
questions.exp: A higher discount rate lowers the present value of future benefits, decreasing the PBO; the decrease is an actuarial gain recognized in OCI and amortized later if it exceeds the corridor. Immediate recognition in income is not required.

questions.q: Kirk Co. recognizes amortization of an accumulated net actuarial loss as a component of net periodic pension cost. What is the effect of this amortization on the funded status and on accumulated other comprehensive income?
choices: Funded status worsens; AOCI is unchanged
Both the funded status and AOCI are unchanged
Funded status is unchanged; the AOCI loss balance decreases
Funded status improves; AOCI loss increases
questions.exp: The loss was already included in the pension liability when it arose. Amortization reclassifies part of it out of AOCI into pension cost (credit OCI, debit pension cost), so the funded status is unchanged and the AOCI loss falls. Treating it as a new increase in the liability double counts it.

questions.q: Lowe Co. purchased nonparticipating annuity contracts to settle a large part of its pension obligation; the settlement cost exceeds the sum of service cost and interest cost for the year. How should Lowe treat the related net loss in AOCI?
choices: Continue to amortize it using the corridor approach
Charge it to retained earnings
Reclassify it to an intangible asset
Recognize a pro rata portion of the net loss in earnings immediately
questions.exp: A settlement that exceeds service cost plus interest cost requires immediate recognition in earnings of the pro rata portion of the unrecognized net gain or loss (ASC 715-30). Corridor amortization applies only when there is no settlement.

questions.q: Mayo Co.'s pension data for the year: service cost $300,000; interest cost $180,000; expected return on plan assets $220,000; amortization of net gain $10,000; amortization of prior service cost $30,000. What is net periodic pension cost?
questions.exp: $300,000 + $180,000 - $220,000 - $10,000 + $30,000 = $280,000. Amortization of a net gain reduces pension cost; adding it gives the $300,000 trap.

questions.q: Nash Co.'s PBO was $6,000,000 at January 1. On that date, a plan amendment granting credit for prior service increased the PBO by $400,000. The discount rate is 6%, and no benefits were paid during the year. What is interest cost for the year?
questions.exp: Interest cost is the discount rate times the PBO outstanding during the period, including the amendment effective January 1: ($6,000,000 + $400,000) x 6% = $384,000. $360,000 omits the obligation added by the amendment.

questions.q: Oak Co.'s defined benefit plan is overfunded: the fair value of plan assets exceeds the PBO. How should Oak present the funded status?
choices: As a noncurrent asset
Split between current and noncurrent assets based on expected benefit payments
As a current asset
Only in the notes, because pension assets belong to the trust
questions.exp: An overfunded plan is recognized as a noncurrent asset (ASC 715-20). Only underfunded plans may have a current liability portion, for benefits payable in the next 12 months that exceed plan assets.

questions.q: Pell Co.'s net periodic pension cost for the year was $400,000, consisting only of service cost, interest cost, and expected return. Actual return equaled expected return, and there were no actuarial gains or losses or plan amendments. Pell contributed $500,000 to the plan. By how much did Pell's net pension liability change?
choices: Decreased by $500,000
Decreased by $100,000
Increased by $100,000
Increased by $400,000
questions.exp: Pension cost of $400,000 increases the net liability, and contributions of $500,000 reduce it, so the net liability decreases by $100,000. Counting only the contribution ignores the cost accrued for the year.

questions.q: Under ASC 715, the expected return on plan assets is computed by applying the expected long-term rate of return to which measure?
choices: The cost basis of plan assets
The projected benefit obligation
The fair value of plan assets at the end of the year
The market-related value of plan assets, which may be fair value or a calculated value that recognizes changes over no more than five years
questions.exp: ASC 715-30 bases the expected return on the market-related value of plan assets, either fair value or a smoothed value recognizing changes in fair value over up to five years. End-of-year fair value already includes the actual return, so it would be circular.

questions.q: On January 1, Year 1, Quay Co. amended its pension plan, creating $600,000 of prior service cost. The average remaining service period of the active employees expected to benefit is 12 years, and Quay uses straight-line amortization. What amount of prior service cost should be amortized into pension cost in Year 1?
questions.exp: $600,000 / 12 years = $50,000 per year, reclassified from AOCI into net periodic cost. Zero would apply only if amortization started in a later year, and expensing $600,000 at once is not permitted.

questions.q: Rand Co.'s unfunded postretirement health care plan had an expected postretirement benefit obligation of $1,500,000, an accumulated postretirement benefit obligation of $900,000, and plan assets of $100,000 at year-end. What liability should Rand recognize for the plan?
questions.exp: For OPEB plans, the funded status is the APBO less plan assets: $900,000 - $100,000 = $800,000 (ASC 715-60). The EPBO includes benefits for service not yet rendered and is not the balance sheet measure.

questions.q: Sung Co., which reports on a calendar year, sponsors a defined benefit plan. As of what date should Sung generally measure plan assets and benefit obligations?
choices: The plan's own fiscal year-end
Its fiscal year-end (with a practical expedient permitting the month-end closest to it)
Any date within three months before year-end
The date of the most recent actuarial valuation
questions.exp: ASC 715-30 requires measurement as of the employer's fiscal year-end, and ASU 2015-04 allows a practical expedient to measure as of the month-end closest to it. The old three-month-earlier option was eliminated.

questions.q: At January 1, Tull Co. had a $400,000 pretax net loss in AOCI related to its pension plan. During the year, it had an asset gain of $50,000, a liability (actuarial) loss of $120,000, and amortization of net loss of $15,000. What is the net loss in AOCI at December 31?
questions.exp: $400,000 - $50,000 gain + $120,000 loss - $15,000 amortization = $455,000. $485,000 adds the amortization, but amortization moves loss out of AOCI into pension cost.

questions.q: Under ASU 2017-07, which component of net periodic pension cost is eligible to be capitalized into inventory or a self-constructed asset?
choices: Amortization of prior service cost
Service cost only
Interest cost
All components
questions.exp: ASU 2017-07 limits capitalization to the service cost component; interest cost, expected return, and amortization amounts cannot be capitalized. Capitalizing all components was permitted before the amendment.

questions.q: Vale Co. closed a division, significantly reducing the expected years of future service of current employees covered by its pension plan. How should Vale account for unamortized prior service cost associated with the years of service no longer expected?
choices: Reclassify it to goodwill
Continue to amortize it over the original period
Charge it to retained earnings
Recognize it as a curtailment loss in earnings
questions.exp: This is a curtailment under ASC 715-30: prior service cost for the years of service no longer expected is recognized immediately as a loss. Continuing normal amortization ignores that the future service has been eliminated.

questions.q: Which relationship among pension obligation measures is always true for a pay-related plan with expected future salary increases?
choices: Accumulated benefit obligation <= vested benefit obligation <= projected benefit obligation
Accumulated benefit obligation = projected benefit obligation
Projected benefit obligation <= accumulated benefit obligation <= vested benefit obligation
Vested benefit obligation <= accumulated benefit obligation <= projected benefit obligation
questions.exp: The VBO counts only vested benefits; the ABO adds nonvested benefits at current pay; the PBO further adds projected salary increases. Equal ABO and PBO occur only in a non-pay-related plan.

questions.q: Wren Co.'s unfunded postretirement health care plan reported the following for the year: service cost $40,000; interest cost $30,000; amortization of prior service cost $5,000; benefits paid to retirees $25,000. What is net periodic postretirement benefit cost?
questions.exp: Net cost = $40,000 + $30,000 + $5,000 = $75,000; an unfunded plan has no expected return. Benefits paid reduce the obligation and cash but are not part of the cost, so $100,000 is wrong.

questions.q: At January 1, Yost Co. had a $300,000 unrecognized net actuarial loss in AOCI. Its PBO was $4,000,000 and the market-related value of plan assets was $3,800,000 on that date; the average remaining service period is 10 years. What amount of net loss must be amortized into pension cost for the year?
questions.exp: The corridor is 10% of the greater of PBO or market-related value, $400,000; the $300,000 net loss falls within it, so no minimum amortization is required (ASC 715-30). $30,000 amortizes the entire loss without applying the corridor.

topics.topic: Property, plant and equipment and depreciation

questions.q: A company bought a parcel of land with an old building for $300,000, intending to raze the building and construct a new office. It paid legal fees of $5,000, title insurance of $2,000, razing costs of $20,000 (salvage sold for $3,000), grading of $8,000, back property taxes assumed of $4,000, parking lot paving of $25,000 and architect fees for the new building of $30,000. What is the cost of the land?
questions.exp: Land = $300,000 + $5,000 + $2,000 + ($20,000 - $3,000) + $8,000 + $4,000 = $336,000. Paving is a depreciable land improvement and architect fees belong to the building; including the paving gives $361,000.

questions.q: A company paid $900,000 for land, a building and equipment. Their fair values were $200,000, $600,000 and $200,000, respectively. At what amount should the building be recorded?
questions.exp: A lump-sum purchase is allocated by relative fair value: $900,000 x $600,000 / $1,000,000 = $540,000. Recording the building at its $600,000 fair value would make total cost exceed the price paid.

questions.q: A company is constructing a building for its own use. Weighted-average accumulated expenditures for the year were $1,000,000. It has a $600,000 construction loan at 8% and other debt of $2,000,000 at a weighted-average rate of 10%. Total interest incurred for the year was $248,000. How much interest should be capitalized?
questions.exp: Avoidable interest = $600,000 x 8% + $400,000 x 10% = $88,000, which is less than actual interest of $248,000 (ASC 835-20). Applying the 10% general rate to all expenditures gives $100,000, ignoring the specific borrowing.

questions.q: A company's weighted-average accumulated expenditures on a self-constructed warehouse were $3,000,000. It had no specific construction borrowing; its only debt was a $1,000,000 note at 9% outstanding all year. How much interest should be capitalized?
questions.exp: Avoidable interest would be $3,000,000 x 9% = $270,000, but capitalized interest cannot exceed actual interest incurred, which is $1,000,000 x 9% = $90,000. Capitalizing the full avoidable amount ignores the actual-interest ceiling.

questions.q: A machine costing $100,000 with a $10,000 salvage value and a five-year life is depreciated using the double-declining-balance method. What is depreciation expense in Year 2?
questions.exp: The DDB rate is 40%; Year 1 = $100,000 x 40% = $40,000 and Year 2 = $60,000 x 40% = $24,000. DDB ignores salvage in computing the base (salvage only limits total depreciation), so using $90,000 as the base gives $36,000 in Year 1 and $21,600 in Year 2.

questions.q: A company purchased equipment on April 1, Year 1 for $64,000. It has a $4,000 salvage value and a five-year life and is depreciated by the sum-of-the-years'-digits method. The company has a calendar year-end. What is depreciation expense for Year 2?
questions.exp: Depreciable base is $60,000 and the SYD denominator is 15. Year 2 spans 3 months of asset-year 1 and 9 months of asset-year 2: $60,000 x 5/15 x 3/12 + $60,000 x 4/15 x 9/12 = $5,000 + $12,000 = $17,000. Using only the second-year fraction gives $16,000.

questions.q: A machine costing $500,000 with a $50,000 residual value is expected to produce 300,000 units. It produced 45,000 units this year. What is depreciation expense under the units-of-production method?
questions.exp: Rate = ($500,000 - $50,000) / 300,000 = $1.50 per unit; depreciation = 45,000 x $1.50 = $67,500. Ignoring residual value gives $75,000.

questions.q: A company bought equipment for $200,000 with a $20,000 salvage value and a 10-year life, depreciated straight-line. At the start of Year 5, it revised the total life to 8 years and the salvage value to $8,000. What is depreciation expense for Year 5?
questions.exp: After four years, carrying amount = $200,000 - 4 x $18,000 = $128,000; Year 5 depreciation = ($128,000 - $8,000) / 4 remaining years = $30,000, applied prospectively under ASC 250. Recomputing from original cost over 8 years ($24,000) treats the change retrospectively.

questions.q: A company exchanged old equipment (cost $80,000, accumulated depreciation $50,000, fair value $40,000) plus $15,000 cash for new equipment. The exchange has commercial substance. At what amount should the new equipment be recorded?
questions.exp: With commercial substance, the new asset is recorded at the fair value of what was given: $40,000 + $15,000 = $55,000, and a $10,000 gain is recognized (ASC 845). Carrying amount plus cash ($45,000) is the treatment when the exchange lacks commercial substance.

questions.q: A company exchanged equipment with a carrying amount of $30,000 and fair value of $40,000 for similar equipment with a fair value of $32,000 plus $8,000 cash. The exchange lacks commercial substance. What gain should be recognized?
questions.exp: When boot received is less than 25% of total consideration ($8,000 / $40,000 = 20%), a proportionate gain is recognized: $10,000 x $8,000 / $40,000 = $2,000 (ASC 845-10-30-6). Recognizing the full $10,000 applies the commercial-substance treatment.

questions.q: A machine used in operations has a carrying amount of $900,000. Because of declining demand, the company tested it for recoverability: its expected undiscounted future cash flows total $950,000, and its fair value is $700,000. What impairment loss should be recognized under ASC 360?
questions.exp: Under ASC 360-10-35-17, a held-and-used asset is impaired only if its carrying amount exceeds the sum of undiscounted cash flows; $900,000 is recoverable from $950,000, so no loss is recognized. Comparing carrying amount directly to fair value ($200,000) skips the recoverability test.

questions.q: A factory group has a $900,000 carrying amount, undiscounted expected cash inflows of $850,000, a fair value of $700,000 and a present value of expected cash flows of $720,000. Using fair value as the measure, what impairment loss is recognized?
questions.exp: The group fails recoverability ($850,000 < $900,000), so the loss is carrying amount less fair value: $900,000 - $700,000 = $200,000. Measuring the loss against undiscounted cash flows ($50,000) confuses the recoverability test with measurement.

questions.q: In Year 1, a company recognized a $100,000 impairment loss on equipment held and used. In Year 2, the equipment's fair value recovered by $60,000. How should the recovery be reported under U.S. GAAP?
choices: Restate Year 1 to reverse the loss
Do not recognize the recovery
Recognize a $60,000 gain in other comprehensive income
Recognize a $60,000 gain in net income
questions.exp: ASC 360-10-35-20 prohibits restoring a previously recognized impairment loss on an asset held and used; the reduced carrying amount is the new cost basis. Reversal is permitted under IFRS (IAS 36), which is the trap.

questions.q: A company classified a building as held for sale when its carrying amount was $500,000 and its fair value less cost to sell was $420,000. At the next reporting date, fair value less cost to sell rose to $470,000. What gain, if any, should be recognized at the next reporting date?
questions.exp: Assets held for sale are measured at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less cost to sell, and later increases are recognized as gains up to the cumulative loss previously recognized ($80,000): $470,000 - $420,000 = $50,000 (ASC 360-10-35-40). Treating it like a held-and-used asset, with no recovery allowed, is the trap.

questions.q: On January 1, a company installed an offshore platform with an expected retirement cost of $1,000,000 in 10 years. Its credit-adjusted risk-free rate is 8%, and the present value factor for 10 years at 8% is 0.4632. What accretion expense on the asset retirement obligation should be recognized in Year 1?
questions.exp: The ARO is initially $1,000,000 x 0.4632 = $463,200, and Year 1 accretion = $463,200 x 8% = $37,056 (ASC 410-20). Spreading the $463,200 evenly ($46,320) confuses depreciation of the capitalized cost with accretion of the liability.

questions.q: During the year, a company spent $40,000 on a major overhaul that extended a machine's useful life, $6,000 on routine repairs, $100,000 on a new wing added to its building and $5,000 repainting offices. How much should be capitalized?
questions.exp: Expenditures that extend useful life or add capacity are capitalized: $40,000 + $100,000 = $140,000. Routine repairs and repainting maintain the assets and are expensed.

questions.q: A city donated land with a fair value of $250,000 to a corporation to induce it to build a plant there. How should the corporation record the land?
choices: At the city's original cost of the land
At $250,000, with a credit to additional paid-in capital from the city
At $0, with disclosure only
At $250,000, with a corresponding gain or contribution revenue in income
questions.exp: A donated asset received in a nonreciprocal transfer is recorded at its fair value, with the credit recognized in income as a gain or contribution revenue. Crediting paid-in capital is outdated practice, and recording at zero ignores an asset the company controls.

questions.q: Equipment costing $120,000 with no salvage value and a 10-year life was purchased on January 1, Year 1 and depreciated straight-line. It was sold on July 1, Year 5 for $70,000. What gain or loss should be recognized on the sale?
choices: $2,000 loss
$4,000 gain
questions.exp: Depreciation through July 1, Year 5 = $12,000 x 4.5 = $54,000; carrying amount = $66,000; gain = $70,000 - $66,000 = $4,000. Omitting the half-year of Year 5 depreciation gives a $72,000 carrying amount and a $2,000 loss.

questions.q: A warehouse with a carrying amount of $300,000 was destroyed by fire. The company received $380,000 from its insurer and plans to reinvest the entire amount in a replacement warehouse. How should the company report the involuntary conversion?
choices: An $80,000 gain in net income
An $80,000 gain in other comprehensive income
An $80,000 reduction in the cost of the replacement warehouse
No gain, because the proceeds will be reinvested
questions.exp: Under ASC 610-30, gains on involuntary conversions of nonmonetary assets to monetary assets are recognized in income even if the proceeds are reinvested. Deferring the gain through reinvestment is a tax rule (IRC Section 1033), not GAAP.

questions.q: A company acquired equipment by issuing a $100,000 noninterest-bearing note payable in two years. The equipment's cash price is not known, and the company's incremental borrowing rate is 10% (two-year present value factor 0.8264). At what amount should the equipment be recorded?
questions.exp: The asset is recorded at the present value of the note: $100,000 x 0.8264 = $82,640, with the $17,360 discount recognized as interest expense over two years (ASC 835-30). Recording at the face amount overstates the asset by including future interest.

questions.q: A company acquired land by issuing 10,000 shares of its $1 par common stock, which is actively traded at $45 per share. An appraiser valued the land at $480,000. At what amount should the land be recorded?
questions.exp: Assets acquired for stock are recorded at the more clearly evident fair value; the quoted price of actively traded stock ($450,000) is more reliable than an appraisal. Par value of $10,000 is not a measure of fair value.

questions.q: A company uses composite depreciation for a group of similar assets. It retires one asset with an original cost of $20,000 and receives $4,000 in salvage proceeds. How should the retirement be recorded?
choices: Recognize a loss equal to the asset's estimated carrying amount less $4,000
Debit cash $4,000 and accumulated depreciation $16,000, and credit the asset $20,000, with no gain or loss
Recognize a gain of $4,000
Recompute the composite rate and adjust prior-year depreciation
questions.exp: Under composite or group depreciation, retirements are charged to accumulated depreciation for the difference between cost and proceeds, with no gain or loss recognized. Computing a gain or loss treats the asset as individually depreciated.

questions.q: Which of the following should NOT be depreciated?
choices: Leasehold improvements
Land, including costs to clear and grade it
Fences surrounding a factory
Paved parking lots
